entries.source: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv93"/><title type="x-ms">Lamentations</title> <div sID="gen18237" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18238" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">Since</hi> what Solomon says, though contrary to the common opinion of the world, is certainly true, that <hi type="italic">sorrow is better than laughter,</hi> and <hi type="italic">it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting,</hi> we should come to the reading and consideration of the melancholy chapters of this book, not only willingly, but with an expectation to edify ourselves by them; and, that we may do this, we must compose ourselves to a holy sadness and resolve to weep with the weeping prophet. Let us consider, I. The title of this book; in the Hebrew it has one, but is called (as the books of Moses are) from the first word <hi type="italic">Ecah</hi>—<hi type="italic">How;</hi> but the Jewish commentators call it, as the Greeks do, and we from them, <hi type="italic">Kinoth</hi>—<hi type="italic">Lamentations.</hi> As we have sacred odes or songs of joy, so have we sacred elegies or songs of lamentation; such variety of methods has Infinite Wisdom taken to work upon us and move our affections, and so soften our hearts and make them susceptible of the impressions of divine truths, as the wax of the seal. We have not only <hi type="italic">piped unto you,</hi> but have <hi type="italic">mourned</hi> likewise, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.17">Matt. xi. 17</reference>. II. The penman of this book; it was Jeremiah the prophet, who is here Jeremiah the poet, and <hi type="italic">vates</hi> signifies both; therefore this book is fitly adjoined to the book of his prophecy, and is as an appendix to it. We had there at large the predictions of the desolations of Judah and Jerusalem, and then the history of them, to show how punctually the predictions were accomplished, for the confirming of our faith: now here we have the expressions of his sorrow upon occasion of them, to show that he was very sincere in the protestations he had often made that he did not desire the woeful day, but that, on the contrary, the prospect of it filled him with bitterness. When he saw these calamities at a distance, he wished that his <hi type="italic">head were waters and his eyes fountains of tears;</hi> and, when they came, he made it to appear that he did not dissemble in that wish, and that he was far from being disaffected to his country, which was the crime his enemies charged him with. Though his country had been very unkind to him, and though the ruin of it was both a proof that he was a true prophet and a punishment of them for prosecuting him as a false prophet, which might have tempted him to rejoice in it, yet he sadly lamented it, and herein showed a better temper than that which Jonah was of with respect to Nineveh. III. The occasion of these Lamentations was the destruction of Judah and Jerusalem by the Chaldean army and the dissolution of the Jewish state both civil and ecclesiastical thereby. Some of the rabbies will have these to be the Lamentations which Jeremiah penned upon occasion of the death of Josiah, which are mentioned <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">2 Chron. xxxv. 25</reference>. But, though it is true that that opened the door to all the following calamities, yet these Lamentations seem to be penned in the sight, not in the foresight, of those calamities—when they had already come, not when they were at a distance; and there is nothing of Josiah in them, and his praise, as was no question, in the lamentations for him. No, it is Jerusalem's funeral that this is an elegy upon. Others of them will have these Lamentations to be contained in the roll which Baruch wrote from Jeremiah's mouth, and which Jehoiakim burnt, and they suggest that at first there were in it only the 1st, 2nd, and 4th chapters, but that the 3rd and 5th were the <hi type="italic">many like words</hi> that were afterwards added; but this is a groundless fancy; that roll is expressly said to be a repetition and summary of the prophet's sermons, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.2">Jer. xxxvi. 2</reference>. IV. The composition of it; it is not only poetical, but alphabetical, all except the 5th chapter, as some of David's psalms are; each verse begins with a several letter in the order of the Hebrew alphabet, the first <hi type="italic">aleph,</hi> the second <hi type="italic">beth,</hi> &c., but the 3rd chapter is a triple alphabet, the first three beginning with <hi type="italic">aleph,</hi> the next three with <hi type="italic">beth,</hi> &c., which was a help to memory (it being designed that these mournful ditties should be got by heart) and was an elegance in writing then valued and therefore not now to be despised. They observe that in the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th chapters, the letter <hi type="italic">pe</hi> is put before <hi type="italic">ain,</hi> which in all the Hebrew alphabets follows it, for a reason of which Dr. Lightfoot offers this conjecture, That the letter <hi type="italic">ajin,</hi> which is the numeral letter for LXX., was thus, by being displaced, made remarkable, to put them in mind of the seventy years at the end of which God would turn again their captivity. V. The use of it: of great use, no doubt, it was to the pious Jews in their sufferings, furnishing them with spiritual language to express their natural grief by, helping to preserve the lively remembrance of Zion among them, and their children that never saw it, when they were in Babylon, directing their tears into the right channel (for they are here taught to mourn for sin and mourn to God), and withal encouraging their hopes that God would yet return and have mercy upon them; and it is of use to us, to affect us with godly sorrow for the calamities of the church of God, as becomes those that are living members of it and are resolved to take our lot with it. <div eID="gen18238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18239" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18240" type="x-p"/> We have here the first alphabet of this lamentation, twenty-two stanzas, in which the miseries of Jerusalem are bitterly bewailed and her present deplorable condition is aggravated by comparing it with her former prosperous state; all along, sin is acknowledged and complained of as the procuring cause of all these miseries; and God is appealed to for justice against their enemies and applied to for compassion towards them. The chapter is all of a piece, and the several remonstrances are interwoven; but here is, I. A complaint made to God of their calamities, and his compassionate consideration desired, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.1-Lam.1.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. The same complaint made to their friends, and their compassionate consideration desired, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.12-Lam.1.17">ver. 12-17</reference>. III. An appeal to God and his righteousness concerning it (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.18-Lam.1.22">ver. 18-22</reference>), in which he is justified in their affliction and is humbly solicited to justify himself in their deliverance. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv93"/> <div eID="gen18240" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18239" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Miseries of Jerusalem; Grief for the Loss of Ordinances. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18241" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> How doth the city sit solitary, <hi type="italic">that was</hi> full of people! <hi type="italic">how</hi> is she become as a widow! she <hi type="italic">that was</hi> great among the nations, <hi type="italic">and</hi> princess among the provinces, <hi type="italic">how</hi> is she become tributary! <hi type="super">2</hi> She weepeth sore in the night, and her tears <hi type="italic">are</hi> on her cheeks: among all her lovers she hath none to comfort <hi type="italic">her:</hi> all her friends have dealt treacherously with her, they are become her enemies. <hi type="super">3</hi> Judah is gone into captivity because of affliction, and because of great servitude: she dwelleth among the heathen, she findeth no rest: all her persecutors overtook her between the straits. <hi type="super">4</hi> The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts: all her gates are desolate: her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted, and she <hi type="italic">is</hi> in bitterness. <hi type="super">5</hi> Her adversaries are the chief, her enemies prosper; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions: her children are gone into captivity before the enemy. <hi type="super">6</hi> And from the daughter of Zion all her beauty is departed: her princes are become like harts <hi type="italic">that</hi> find no pasture, and they are gone without strength before the pursuer. <hi type="super">7</hi> Jerusalem remembered in the days of her affliction and of her miseries all her pleasant things that she had in the days of old, when her people fell into the hand of the enemy, and none did help her: the adversaries saw her, <hi type="italic">and</hi> did mock at her sabbaths. <hi type="super">8</hi> Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she is removed: all that honoured her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness: yea, she sigheth, and turneth backward. <hi type="super">9</hi> Her filthiness <hi type="italic">is</hi> in her skirts; she remembereth not her last end; therefore she came down wonderfully: she had no comforter<hi type="small-caps">. O Lord</hi> , behold my affliction: for the enemy hath magnified <hi type="italic">himself.</hi> <hi type="super">10</hi> The adversary hath spread out his hand upon all her pleasant things: for she hath seen <hi type="italic">that</hi> the heathen entered into her sanctuary, whom thou didst command <hi type="italic">that</hi> they should not enter into thy congregation. <hi type="super">11</hi> All her people sigh, they seek bread; they have given their pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul: see, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and consider; for I am become vile. <div eID="gen18241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18242" type="x-p"/> Those that have any disposition to <hi type="italic">weep with those that weep,</hi> one would think, should scarcely be able to refrain from tears at the reading of these verses, so very pathetic are the lamentations here. <div eID="gen18242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18243" type="x-p"/> I. The miseries of Jerusalem are here complained of as very pressing and by many circumstances very much aggravated. Let us take a view of these miseries. <div eID="gen18243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18244" type="x-p"/> 1. As to their civil state. (1.) A city that was populous is now depopulated, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.1">v. 1</reference>. It is spoken of by way of wonder—Who would have thought that ever it should come to this! Or by way of enquiry—What is it that has brought it to this? Or by way of lamentation—Alas! alas! (as <reference osisRef="Rev.18.10">Rev. xviii. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.16">16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.19">19</reference>) <hi type="italic">how doth the city sit solitary that was full of people!</hi> She was full of her own people that replenished her, and full of the people of other nations that resorted to her, with whom she had both profitable commerce and pleasant converse; but now her own people are carried into captivity, and strangers make no court to her: she <hi type="italic">sits solitary.</hi> The <hi type="italic">chief places of the city</hi> are not now, as they used to be, <hi type="italic">place of concourse,</hi> where <hi type="italic">wisdom cried</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.20-Prov.1.21">Prov. i. 20, 21</reference>); and justly are they left unfrequented, because wisdom's cry there was not heard. Note, Those that are ever so much increased God can soon diminish. <hi type="italic">How has she become as a widow!</hi> Her king that was, or should have been, as a husband to her, is cut off, and gone; her God has departed from her, and has given her a bill of divorce; she is emptied of her children, is solitary and sorrowful as a widow. Let no family, no state, not Jerusalem, no, nor Babylon herself, be secure, and say, <hi type="italic">I sit as a queen,</hi> and shall never <hi type="italic">sit as a widow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.47.8">Isa. xlvii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.7">Rev. xviii. 7</reference>. (2.) A city that had dominion is now in subjection. She had been <hi type="italic">great among the nations,</hi> greatly loved by some and greatly feared by others, and greatly observed and obeyed by both; some made her presents, and others paid her taxes; so that she was really <hi type="italic">princess among the provinces,</hi> and every sheaf bowed to hers; even the princes of the people entreated her favour. But now the tables are turned; she has not only lost her friends and <hi type="italic">sits solitary,</hi> but has lost her freedom too and sits <hi type="italic">tributary;</hi> she paid tribute to Egypt first and then to Babylon. Note, Sin brings a people not only into solitude, but into slavery. (3.) A city that used to be full of mirth has now become melancholy and upon all accounts full of grief. Jerusalem had been a joyous city, whither the tribes went up on purpose to rejoice before the Lord; she was <hi type="italic">the joy of the whole earth,</hi> but now <hi type="italic">she weeps sorely,</hi> her laughter is turned into mourning, her solemn feasts are all gone; she weeps <hi type="italic">in the night,</hi> as true mourners do who weep in secret, in silence and solitude; <hi type="italic">in the night,</hi> when others compose themselves to rest, her thoughts are most intent upon her troubles, and grief then plays the tyrant. What the prophet's head was for her, when she regarded it not, now her head is—<hi type="italic">as waters, and</hi> her <hi type="italic">eyes fountains of tears,</hi> so that she <hi type="italic">weeps day and night</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.1">Jer. ix. 1</reference>); <hi type="italic">her tears are</hi> continually <hi type="italic">on her cheeks.</hi> Though nothing dries away sooner than a tear, yet fresh griefs extort fresh tears, so that her cheeks are never free from them. Note, There is nothing more commonly seen <hi type="italic">under the sun</hi> than <hi type="italic">the tears of the oppressed,</hi> with whom <hi type="italic">the clouds return after the rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Eccl. iv. 1</reference>. (4.) Those that were separated from the heathen now <hi type="italic">dwell among the heathen;</hi> those that were a peculiar people are now a mingled people (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Judah has gone into captivity,</hi> out of her own land into the land of her enemies, and there she abides, and is likely to abide, among those that are aliens to God and the covenants of promise, with whom <hi type="italic">she finds no rest,</hi> no satisfaction of mind, nor any settlement of abode, but is continually hurried from place to place at the will of the victorious imperious tyrants. And again (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Her children have gone into captivity before the enemy;</hi> those that were to have been the seed of the next generation are carried off; so that the land that is now desolate is likely to be still desolate and lost for want of heirs." Those that dwell among their own people, and that are a free people, and in their own land, would be more thankful for the mercies they thereby enjoy if they would but consider the miseries of those that are forced into strange countries. (5.) Those that used in their wars to conquer are now conquered and triumphed over: <hi type="italic">All her persecutors overlook her between the straits</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.3">v. 3</reference>); they gained all possible advantages against her, sot hat her people unavoidably <hi type="italic">fell into the hand of the enemy,</hi> for there was no way to escape (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.7">v. 7</reference>); they were hemmed in on every side, and, which way soever they attempted to flee, they found themselves embarrassed. When they made the best of their way they could make nothing of it, but were overtaken and overcome; so that every where <hi type="italic">her adversaries are the chief and her enemies prosper</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.5">v. 5</reference>); which way soever their sword turns they get the better. Such straits do men bring themselves into by sin. If we allow that which is our greatest adversary and enemy to have dominion over us, and to be chief in us, justly will our other enemies be suffered to have dominion over us. (6.) Those that had been not only a distinguished but a dignified people, on whom God had put honour, and to whom all their neighbours had paid respect, are now brought into contempt (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that honoured her</hi> before <hi type="italic">despise her;</hi> those that courted an alliance with her now value it not; those that caressed her when she was in pomp and prosperity slight her now that she is in distress, <hi type="italic">because they have seen her nakedness.</hi> By the prevalency of the enemies against her they perceive her weakness, and that she is not so strong a people as they thought she had been; and by the prevalency of God's judgments against her they perceive her wickedness, which now comes to light and is every where talked of. Now it appears how they have vilified themselves by their sins: <hi type="italic">The enemies magnify themselves</hi> against them (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">v. 9</reference>); they trample upon them, and insult over them, and in their eyes they have <hi type="italic">become vile,</hi> the tail of the nations, though once they were the head. Note, <hi type="italic">Sin is the reproach of any people.</hi> (7.) Those that lived in a fruitful land were ready to perish, and many of them did perish, for want of necessary food (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">All her people sigh</hi> in despondency and despair; they are ready to faint away; their spirits fail, and therefore they sigh, <hi type="italic">for they seek bread</hi> and seek it in vain. They were brought at last to that extremity that there was <hi type="italic">no bread for the people of the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.6">Jer. lii. 6</reference>), and in their captivity they had much ado to get break, <reference osisRef="Lam.5.6">ch. v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">They have given their pleasant things,</hi> their jewels and pictures, and all the furniture of their closets and cabinets, which they used to please themselves with looking upon, they have sold these to buy bread for themselves and their families, have parted with them <hi type="italic">for meat to relieve the soul,</hi> or (as the margin is) <hi type="italic">to make the soul come again,</hi> when they were ready to faint away. They desired no other cordial than meat. <hi type="italic">All that a man has will he give for life,</hi> and for bread, which is the staff of life. Let those that abound in pleasant things not be proud of them, nor fond of them; for the time may come when they may be glad to let them go for necessary things. And let those that have competent food to relieve their soul be content with it, and thankful for it, though they have not pleasant things. <div eID="gen18244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18245" type="x-p"/> 2. We have here an account of their miseries in their ecclesiastical state, the ruin of their sacred interest, which was much more to be lamented than that of their secular concerns. (1.) Their religious feasts were no more observed, no more frequented (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The ways of Zion do mourn;</hi> they look melancholy, overgrown with grass and weeds. It used to be a pleasant diversion to see people continually passing and repassing in the highway that led to the temple, but now you may stand there long enough, and see nobody stir; for <hi type="italic">none come to the solemn feasts;</hi> a full end is put to them by the destruction of that which was the <hi type="italic">city of our solemnities,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.20">Isa. xxxiii. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">The solemn feasts</hi> had been neglected and profaned (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.11-Isa.1.12">Isa. i. 11, 12</reference>), and therefore justly is an end now put to them. But, when thus <hi type="italic">the ways of Zion</hi> are made to <hi type="italic">mourn,</hi> all the sons of Zion cannot but mourn with them. It is very grievous to good men to see religious assemblies broken up and scattered, and those restrained from them that would gladly attend them. And, as <hi type="italic">the ways of Zion mourned,</hi> so <hi type="italic">the gates of Zion,</hi> in which the faithful worshippers used to meet, <hi type="italic">are desolate;</hi> for there is none to meet in them. Time was when <hi type="italic">the Lord loved the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob,</hi> but now he has forsaken them, and is provoked to withdraw from them, and therefore it cannot but fare with them as it did with the temple when Christ quitted it. <hi type="italic">Behold, your house is left unto you desolate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Matt. xxiii. 38</reference>. (2.) Their religious persons were quite disabled from performing their wonted services, were quite dispirited: <hi type="italic">Her priests sigh</hi> for the desolations of the temple; their songs are turned into sighs; they sigh, for they have nothing to do, and therefore there is nothing to be had; they sigh, as the people (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">for want of bread,</hi> because the offerings of the Lord, which were their livelihood, failed. It is time to sigh when the priests, the Lord's ministers, sigh. <hi type="italic">Her virgins</hi> also, that used, with their music and dancing, to grace the solemnities of their feasts, <hi type="italic">are afflicted</hi> and <hi type="italic">in heaviness.</hi> Notice is taken of their service in the day of Zion's prosperity (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.25">Ps. lxviii. 25</reference>, <hi type="italic">Among them were the damsels playing with timbrels</hi>), and therefore notice is taken of the failing of it now. <hi type="italic">Her virgins are afflicted,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">she is in bitterness;</hi> that is, all the inhabitants of Zion are so, whose character it is that they are <hi type="italic">sorrowful for the solemn assembly,</hi> and that to them <hi type="italic">the reproach of it is a burden,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.18">Zeph. iii. 18</reference>. (3.) Their religious places were profaned (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The heathen entered into her sanctuary,</hi> into the temple itself, into which no Israelite was permitted to enter, though ever so reverently and devoutly, but the priests only. <hi type="italic">The stranger that comes nigh,</hi> even to worship there, <hi type="italic">shall be put to death.</hi> Thither the heathen now crowds rudely in, not to worship, but to plunder. God had commanded that <hi type="italic">the heathen should not</hi> so much as <hi type="italic">enter into the congregation,</hi> nor be incorporated with the people of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.3">Deut. xxiii. 3</reference>); yet now they <hi type="italic">enter into the sanctuary</hi> without control. Note, Nothing is more grievous to those who have a true concern for the glory of God, nor is more lamented, than the violation of God's laws, and the contempt they see put upon sacred things. What <hi type="italic">the enemy did wickedly in the sanctuary</hi> was complained of, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.3-Ps.74.4">Ps. lxxiv. 3, 4</reference>. (4.) Their religious utensils, and all the rich things with which the temple was adorned and beautified, and which were made use of in the worship of God, were made a prey to the enemy (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The adversary has spread out his hand upon all her pleasant things,</hi> has grasped them all, seized them all, for himself. What these pleasant things are we may learn from <reference osisRef="Isa.64.11">Isa. lxiv. 11</reference>, where, to the complaint of the burning of the temple, it is added, <hi type="italic">All our pleasant things are laid waste;</hi> the ark and the altar, and all the other tokens of God's presence with them, these were their pleasant things above any other things, and these were now broken to pieces and carried away. Thus from <hi type="italic">the daughter of Zion all her beauty has departed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">The beauty of holiness</hi> was the <hi type="italic">beauty of the daughter of Zion;</hi> when the temple, that holy and beautiful house, was destroyed, her beauty was gone; that was the breaking of <hi type="italic">the staff of beauty,</hi> the taking away of the pledges and seals of the covenant, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.10">Zech. xi. 10</reference>. (5.) Their religious days were made a jest of (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The adversaries saw her, and did mock at her sabbaths.</hi> They laughed at them for observing one day in seven as a day of rest from worldly business. Juvenal, a heathen poet, ridicules the Jews in his time for losing a seventh part of their time:— <div eID="gen18245" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen18246"/> <l level="1" sID="gen18247"/>————cui septima quæque fuit lux<l eID="gen18247" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen18248"/>Ignava et vitæ partem non attigit ullam——<l eID="gen18248" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen18249"/>They keep their sabbaths to their cost,<l eID="gen18249" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen18250"/>For thus one day in sev'n is lost;<l eID="gen18250" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen18246"/> <div sID="gen18251" type="x-p"/> II. The sins of Jerusalem are here complained of as the procuring provoking cause of all these calamities. Whoever are the instruments, God is the author of all these troubles; it is <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> that <hi type="italic">has afflicted her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.5">v. 5</reference>) and he has done it as a righteous Judge, for <hi type="italic">she has sinned.</hi> 1. Her sins are for number numberless. Are her troubles many? Her sins are many more. it is <hi type="italic">for the multitude of her transgressions</hi> that <hi type="italic">the Lord has afflicted her.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Jer.30.14">Jer. xxx. 14</reference>. When the transgressions of a people are multiplied we cannot say, as Job does in his own case, that <hi type="italic">wounds are multiplied without cause,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.9.17">Job ix. 17</reference>. 2. They are for nature exceedingly heinous (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Jerusalem has grievously sinned,</hi> has <hi type="italic">sinned sin</hi> (so the word is), sinned wilfully, deliberately, has sinned that sin which of all others is the abominable things that the Lord hates, the sin of idolatry. The sins of Jerusalem, that makes such a profession and enjoys such privileges, are of all others the most grievous sins. She has <hi type="italic">sinned grievously</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">v. 8</reference>), and therefore (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">v. 9</reference>) she <hi type="italic">came down wonderfully.</hi> Note, Grievous sins bring wondrous ruin; there are some workers of iniquity to whom there is a strange punishment, <reference osisRef="Job.31.3">Job xxxi. 3</reference>. They are such sins as may plainly be read in the punishment. (1.) They have been very oppressive and therefore are justly oppressed (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Judah has gone into captivity,</hi> and it is <hi type="italic">because of affliction and great servitude,</hi> because the rich among them afflicted the poor and made them serve with rigour, and particularly (as the Chaldee paraphrases it) because they had oppressed their Hebrew servants, which is charged upon them, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.11">Jer. xxxiv. 11</reference>. Oppression was one of their crying sins (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.6-Jer.6.7">Jer. vi. 6, 7</reference>) and it is a sin that cries aloud. (2.) They have made themselves vile, and therefore are justly vilified. They all <hi type="italic">despise her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">v. 8</reference>), for <hi type="italic">her filthiness is in her skirts;</hi> it appears upon her garments that she has rolled them in the mire of sin. None could stain our glory if we did not stain it ourselves. (3.) They have been very secure and therefore are justly surprised with this ruin (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">She remembers not her last end;</hi> she did not take the warning that was given her to <hi type="italic">consider her latter end,</hi> to consider what would be the end of such wicked courses as she took, and therefore she <hi type="italic">came down wonderfully,</hi> in an astonishing manner, that she might be made to feel what she would not fear; therefore God shall <hi type="italic">make their plagues wonderful.</hi> <div eID="gen18251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18252" type="x-p"/> III. Jerusalem's friends are here complained of as false and faint-hearted, and very unkind: They <hi type="italic">have all dealt treacherously with her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.2">v. 2</reference>), so that, in effect, <hi type="italic">they have become her enemies.</hi> Her deceivers have created her as much vexation as her destroyers. The staff that breaks under us may do us as great a mischief as the <hi type="italic">staff that beats us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.6-Ezek.29.7">Ezek. xxix. 6, 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Her princes,</hi> that should have protected her, have not courage enough to make head against the enemy for their own preservation; they <hi type="italic">are like harts,</hi> that, upon the first alarm, betake themselves to flight and make no resistance; nay, they <hi type="italic">are like harts</hi> that are famished for want of <hi type="italic">pasture,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">are gone without strength before the pursuer,</hi> and, having no strength for flight, are soon run down and made a prey of. Her neighbours are unneighbourly, for, 1. There is none <hi type="italic">to help her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.7">v. 7</reference>); either they could not or they would not; nay, 2. <hi type="italic">She has not comforter,</hi> none to sympathize with her, or suggest any thing to alleviate her griefs, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.7">v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">9</reference>. Like Job's friends, they saw it was to no purpose, her <hi type="italic">grief was so great;</hi> and <hi type="italic">miserable comforters were they all</hi> in such a case. <div eID="gen18252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18253" type="x-p"/> IV. Jerusalem's God is here complained to concerning all these things, and all is referred to his compassionate consideration (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O Lord! behold my affliction,</hi> and take cognizance of it;" and (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">v. 11</reference>), "<hi type="italic">See, O Lord! and consider,</hi> take order about it." Note, The only way to make ourselves easy under our burdens is to cast them upon God first, and leave it to him to do with us as seemeth him good.

<div eID="gen18253" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God Acknowledged in Affliction; Jerusalem's Complaint. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18254" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow, which is done unto me, wherewith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath afflicted <hi type="italic">me</hi> in the day of his fierce anger. <hi type="super">13</hi> From above hath he sent fire into my bones, and it prevaileth against them: he hath spread a net for my feet, he hath turned me back: he hath made me desolate <hi type="italic">and</hi> faint all the day. <hi type="super">14</hi> The yoke of my transgressions is bound by his hand: they are wreathed, <hi type="italic">and</hi> come up upon my neck: he hath made my strength to fall, the Lord hath delivered me into <hi type="italic">their</hi> hands, <hi type="italic">from whom</hi> I am not able to rise up. <hi type="super">15</hi> The Lord hath trodden under foot all my mighty <hi type="italic">men</hi> in the midst of me: he hath called an assembly against me to crush my young men: the Lord hath trodden the virgin, the daughter of Judah, <hi type="italic">as</hi> in a winepress. <hi type="super">16</hi> For these <hi type="italic">things</hi> I weep; mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water, because the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me: my children are desolate, because the enemy prevailed. <hi type="super">17</hi> Zion spreadeth forth her hands, <hi type="italic">and there is</hi> none to comfort her: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath commanded concerning Jacob, <hi type="italic">that</hi> his adversaries <hi type="italic">should be</hi> round about him: Jerusalem is as a menstruous woman among them. <hi type="super">18</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> is righteous; for I have rebelled against his commandment: hear, I pray you, all people, and behold my sorrow: my virgins and my young men are gone into captivity. <hi type="super">19</hi> I called for my lovers, <hi type="italic">but</hi> they deceived me: my priests and mine elders gave up the ghost in the city, while they sought their meat to relieve their souls. <hi type="super">20</hi> Behold, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> in distress: my bowels are troubled; mine heart is turned within me; for I have grievously rebelled: abroad the sword bereaveth, at home <hi type="italic">there is</hi> as death. <hi type="super">21</hi> They have heard that I sigh: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none to comfort me: all mine enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that thou hast done <hi type="italic">it:</hi> thou wilt bring the day <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou hast called, and they shall be like unto me. <hi type="super">22</hi> Let all their wickedness come before thee; and do unto them, as thou hast done unto me for all my transgressions: for my sighs <hi type="italic">are</hi> many, and my heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> faint. <div eID="gen18254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18255" type="x-p"/> The complaints here are, for substance, the same with those in the foregoing part of the chapter; but in these verses the prophet, in the name of the lamenting church, does more particularly acknowledge the hand of god in these calamities, and the righteousness of his hand. <div eID="gen18255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18256" type="x-p"/> I. The church in distress here magnifies her affliction, and yet no more than there was cause for; her groaning was not heavier than her strokes. She appeals to all spectators: <hi type="italic">See if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.12">v. 12</reference>. This might perhaps be truly said of Jerusalem's griefs; but we are apt to apply it too sensibly to ourselves when we are in trouble and more than there is cause for. Because we feel most from our own burden, and cannot be persuaded to reconcile ourselves to it, we are ready to cry out, Surely never was <hi type="italic">sorrow like unto our sorrow;</hi> whereas, if our troubles were to be thrown into a common stock with those of others, and then an equal dividend made, share and share alike, rather than stand to that we should each of us say, "Pray, give me my own again." <div eID="gen18256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18257" type="x-p"/> II. She here looks beyond the instruments to the author of her troubles, and owns them all to be directed, determined, and disposed of by him: "It is <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> that <hi type="italic">has afflicted me,</hi> and he has <hi type="italic">afflicted me</hi> because he is angry with me; the greatness of his displeasure may be measured by the greatness of my distress; it is <hi type="italic">in the day of his fierce anger,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Lam.2.12">v. 12</reference>. Afflictions cannot but be very much our griefs when we see them arising from God's wrath; so the church does here. 1. She is as one in a fever, and the fever is of God's sending: "<hi type="italic">He has sent fire into my bones</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.13">v. 13</reference>), a preternatural heat, which <hi type="italic">prevails against them,</hi> so that they are <hi type="italic">burnt like a hearth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.3">Ps. cii. 3</reference>), pained and wasted, and dried away." 2. She is as one in a net, which the more he struggles to get out of the more he is entangled in, and this net is of God's spreading. "The enemies could not have succeeded in their stratagems had not God <hi type="italic">spread a net for my feet.</hi>" 3. She is as one in a wilderness, whose way is embarrassed, solitary, and tiresome: "<hi type="italic">He has turned me back,</hi> that I cannot go on, <hi type="italic">has made me desolate,</hi> that I have nothing to support me with, but am <hi type="italic">faint all the day.</hi>" 4. She is as one in a yoke, not yoked for service, but for penance, tied neck and heels together (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">The yoke of my transgressions is bound by his hand.</hi> Observe, We never are entangled in any yoke but what is framed out of our own transgressions. The sinner is <hi type="italic">holden with the cords of his own sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.22">Prov. v. 22</reference>. The yoke of Christ's commands is an <hi type="italic">easy yoke</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.30">Matt. xi. 30</reference>), but that of our own transgressions is a heavy one. God is said to bind this yoke when he charges guilt upon us, and brings us into those inward and outward troubles which our sins have deserved; when conscience, as his deputy, binds us over to his judgment, then <hi type="italic">the yoke is bound</hi> and <hi type="italic">wreathed by the hand</hi> of his justice, and nothing but the hand of his pardoning mercy will unbind it. 5. She is as one in the dirt, and he it is that has <hi type="italic">trodden under foot all her mighty men,</hi> that has disabled them to stand, and overthrown them by one judgment after another, and so left them to be trampled upon by their proud conquerors, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">v. 15</reference>. Nay, she is as one in a wine-press, not only trodden down, but trodden to pieces, crushed as grapes in the wine-press of God's wrath, and her blood pressed out as wine, and it is God that has thus <hi type="italic">trodden the virgin, the daughter of Judah.</hi> 6. She is in the hand of her enemies, and it is the Lord that has delivered her <hi type="italic">into their hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">He has made my strength to fall,</hi> so that <hi type="italic">I am not able to</hi> make head against them; nay, not only not able to rise up against them, but <hi type="italic">not able to rise up</hi> from them, and then <hi type="italic">he has delivered me into their hands;</hi> nay (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">v. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">he has called an assembly against me, to crush my young men,</hi> and such an assembly as it is in vain to think of opposing; and again (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Lord has commanded concerning Jacob that his adversaries should be round about him.</hi> He that has many a time <hi type="italic">commanded deliverances for Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.4">Ps. xliv. 4</reference>) now commands an invasion against Jacob, because Jacob has disobeyed the commands of his law. <div eID="gen18257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18258" type="x-p"/> III. She justly demands a share in the pity and compassion of those that were the spectators of her misery (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Is it nothing to you, all you that pass by?</hi> Can you look upon me without concern? What! are your hearts as adamants and your eyes as marbles, that you cannot bestow upon me one compassionate thought, or look, or tear? Are not you also in the body? Is it nothing to you that your neighbor's house is on fire?" There are those to whom Zion's sorrows and ruins are nothing; they are not <hi type="italic">grieved for the affliction of Joseph.</hi> How pathetically does she beg their compassion! (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Hear, I pray you, all people, and behold my sorrow:</hi> hear my complaints, and see what cause I have for them." This is a request like that of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.19.21">ch. xix. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O you my friends!</hi> It helps to make a burden sit lighter if our friends sympathize with us, and mingle their tears with ours, for this is an evidence that, though we are in affliction, we are not in contempt, which is commonly as much dreaded in an affliction as any thing. <div eID="gen18258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18259" type="x-p"/> IV. She justifies her own grief, though it was very extreme, for these calamities (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">For these things I weep,</hi> I weep in the night (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.2">v. 2</reference>), when none sees; <hi type="italic">my eye, my eye, runs down with water.</hi>" Note, This world is a vale of tears to the people of God. Zion's sons are often Zion's mourners. <hi type="italic">Zion spreads forth her hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">v. 17</reference>), which is here an expression rather of despair than of desire; she flings out her hands as giving up all for gone. Let us see how she accounts for this passionate grief. 1. Her God has withdrawn from her; and Micah, that had but gods of gold, when they were stolen from him cried out, <hi type="italic">What have I more? And what is it that you say unto me? What aileth thee?</hi> The church here grieves excessively; for, says she, <hi type="italic">the comforter that should relieve my soul is far from me.</hi> God is the comforter; he used to be so to her; he only can administer effectual comforts; it is his word that speaks them; it is his Spirit that speaks them to us. His are strong consolations, able to <hi type="italic">relieve the soul,</hi> to <hi type="italic">bring it back</hi> when it is gone, and we cannot of ourselves <hi type="italic">fetch it again;</hi> but now he has departed in displeasure, he is <hi type="italic">far from me,</hi> and beholds me <hi type="italic">afar off.</hi> Note, It is no marvel that the souls of the saints faint away, when God, who is the only Comforter that can relieve them, keeps at a distance. 2. Her children are removed from her, and are in no capacity to help her: it is for them that she weeps, as Rachel for hers, <hi type="italic">because they were not,</hi> and therefore she <hi type="italic">refuses to be comforted. Her children were desolate, because the enemy prevailed</hi> against them; there is <hi type="italic">none of all her sons to take her by the hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.18">Isa. li. 18</reference>); they cannot help themselves, and how should they help her? Both the damsels and the youths, that were her joy and hope, <hi type="italic">have gone into captivity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.18">v. 18</reference>. It is said of the Chaldeans that they had <hi type="italic">no compassion upon young men nor maidens,</hi> not on the fair sex, not on the blooming age, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.17">2 Chron. xxxvi. 17</reference>. 3. Her friends failed her; some would not and others could not give her any relief. She <hi type="italic">spread forth her hands,</hi> as begging relief, but <hi type="italic">there is none to comfort her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">v. 17</reference>), none that can do it, none that cares to do it; she <hi type="italic">called</hi> for her <hi type="italic">lovers,</hi> and, to engage them to help her, <hi type="italic">called</hi> them her <hi type="italic">lovers,</hi> but they <hi type="italic">deceived</hi> her (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.19">v. 19</reference>), they proved like the brooks in summer to the thirsty traveller, <reference osisRef="Job.6.15">Job vi. 15</reference>. Note, Those creatures that we set our hearts upon and raise our expectations from we are commonly deceived and disappointed in. Her idols were her lovers. Egypt and Assyria were her confidants. But they deceived her. Those that made court to her in her prosperity were shy of her, and strange to her, in her adversity. Happy are those that have made God their friend and keep themselves in his love, for he will not deceive them! 4. Those whose office it was to guide her were disabled from doing her any service. The <hi type="italic">priests</hi> and the <hi type="italic">elders,</hi> that should have appeared at the head of affairs, died for hunger (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.19">v. 19</reference>); they <hi type="italic">gave up the ghost,</hi> or were ready to expire, <hi type="italic">while they sought their meat;</hi> they went a begging for bread to keep them alive. <hi type="italic">The famine</hi> is <hi type="italic">sore</hi> indeed <hi type="italic">in the land</hi> when there is no bread to the wise, when priests and elders are starved. The priests and elders should have been her comforters; but how should they comfort others when they themselves were comfortless? "<hi type="italic">They have heard that I sigh,</hi> which should have summoned them to my assistance; but <hi type="italic">there is none to comfort me. Lover and friend hast thou put far from me.</hi>" 5. Her enemies were too hard for her, and they insulted over her; they have <hi type="italic">prevailed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">v. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Abroad the sword bereaves</hi> and slays all that comes in its way, and <hi type="italic">at home</hi> all provisions are cut off by the besiegers, so that <hi type="italic">there is as death,</hi> that is, famine, which is as bad as the pestilence, or worse—<hi type="italic">the sword without and terror within,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.25">Deut. xxxii. 25</reference>. And as the enemies, that were the instruments of the calamity, were very barbarous, so were those that were the standers by, the Edomites and Ammonites, that bore ill will to Israel: They have <hi type="italic">heard of my trouble, and are glad that thou hast done it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.21">v. 21</reference>); they rejoice in the trouble itself; they rejoice that it is God's doing; it pleases them to find that God and his Israel have fallen out, and they act accordingly with a great deal of strangeness towards them. <hi type="italic">Jerusalem is as a menstruous woman among them,</hi> that they are afraid of touching and are shy of, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">v. 17</reference>. Upon all these accounts it cannot be wondered at, nor can she be blamed, that <hi type="italic">her sighs are many,</hi> in grieving for what is, and that <hi type="italic">her heart is faint</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.22">v. 22</reference>) in fear of what is yet further likely to be. <div eID="gen18259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18260" type="x-p"/> V. She justifies God in all that is brought upon her, acknowledging that her sins had deserved these severe chastenings. The yoke that lies so heavily, and binds so hard, is <hi type="italic">the yoke of her transgressions,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.14">v. 14</reference>. The fetters we are held in are of our own making, and it is with our own rod that we are beaten. When the church had spoken here as if she thought the Lord severe she does well to correct herself, at least to explain herself, but acknowledging (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.18">v. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Lord is righteous.</hi> He does us no wrong in dealing thus with us, nor can we charge him with any injustice in it; how unrighteous soever men are, we are sure that the <hi type="italic">Lord is righteous,</hi> and manifests his justice, though they contradict all the laws of theirs. Note, Whatever our troubles are, which God is pleased to inflict upon us, we must own that therein he <hi type="italic">is righteous;</hi> we understand neither him nor ourselves if we do not own it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.6">2 Chron. xii. 6</reference>. She owns the equity of God's actions, but owning the iniquity of her own: <hi type="italic">I have rebelled against his commandments</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.18">v. 18</reference>); and again (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have grievously rebelled.</hi> We cannot speak ill enough of sin, and we must always speak worst of our own sin, must call it <hi type="italic">rebellion, grievous rebellion;</hi> and very grievous sins is to all true penitents. It is this that lies more heavily upon her than the afflictions she was under: "<hi type="italic">My bowels are troubled;</hi> they work within me as the troubled sea; <hi type="italic">my heart is turned within me,</hi> is restless, is turned upside down; <hi type="italic">for I have grievously rebelled.</hi>" Note, Sorrow for our sin must be great sorrow and must affect the soul. <div eID="gen18260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18261" type="x-p"/> VI. She appeals both to the mercy and to the justice of God in her present case. 1. She appeals to the mercy of God concerning her own sorrows, which had made her the proper object of his compassion (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Behold, O Lord! for I am in distress;</hi> take cognizance of my case, and take such order for my relief as thou pleasest." Note, It is matter of comfort to us that the troubles which oppress our spirits are open before God's eye. 2. She appeals to the justice of God concerning the injuries that her enemies did her (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.21-Lam.2.22">v. 21, 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou wilt bring the day that thou hast called,</hi> the day that is fixed in the counsels of God and published in the prophecies, when my enemies, that now prosecute me, <hi type="italic">shall be made like unto me,</hi> when the cup of trembling, now put into my hands, shall be put into theirs." It may be read as a prayer, "Let the day appointed come," and so it goes on, "<hi type="italic">Let their wickedness come before thee,</hi> let it come to be remembered, let it come to be reckoned for; take vengeance on them for all the wrongs they have done to me (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.14-Ps.109.15">Ps. cix. 14, 15</reference>); hasten the time when thou wilt <hi type="italic">do to them</hi> for their transgressions <hi type="italic">as thou hast done to me</hi> for mine." This prayer amounts to a protestation against all thoughts of a coalition with them, and to a prediction of their ruin, subscribing to that which God had in his word spoken of it. Note, Our prayers may and must agree with God's word; and what day God has here called we are to call for, and no other. And though we are bound in charity to forgive our enemies, and to pray for them, yet we may in faith pray for the accomplishment of that which God has spoken against his and his church's enemies, that will not repent to give him glory.  <chapter eID="Lam.1"/> <div eID="gen18261" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen18264" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18263" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Cause, Extent, and Greatness of Zion's Calamities. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18265" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> How hath the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud in his anger, <hi type="italic">and</hi> cast down from heaven unto the earth the beauty of Israel, and remembered not his footstool in the day of his anger! <hi type="super">2</hi> The Lord hath swallowed up all the habitations of Jacob, and hath not pitied: he hath thrown down in his wrath the strong holds of the daughter of Judah; he hath brought <hi type="italic">them</hi> down to the ground: he hath polluted the kingdom and the princes thereof. <hi type="super">3</hi> He hath cut off in <hi type="italic">his</hi> fierce anger all the horn of Israel: he hath drawn back his right hand from before the enemy, and he burned against Jacob like a flaming fire, <hi type="italic">which</hi> devoureth round about. <hi type="super">4</hi> He hath bent his bow like an enemy: he stood with his right hand as an adversary, and slew all <hi type="italic">that were</hi> pleasant to the eye in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion: he poured out his fury like fire. <hi type="super">5</hi> The Lord was as an enemy: he hath swallowed up Israel, he hath swallowed up all her palaces: he hath destroyed his strong holds, and hath increased in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he hath violently taken away his tabernacle, as <hi type="italic">if it were of</hi> a garden: he hath destroyed his places of the assembly: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath caused the solemn feasts and sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, and hath despised in the indignation of his anger the king and the priest. <hi type="super">7</hi> The Lord hath cast off his altar, he hath abhorred his sanctuary, he hath given up into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces; they have made a noise in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , as in the day of a solemn feast. <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together. <hi type="super">9</hi> Her gates are sunk into the ground; he hath destroyed and broken her bars: her king and her princes <hi type="italic">are</hi> among the Gentiles: the law <hi type="italic">is</hi> no <hi type="italic">more;</hi> her prophets also find no vision from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18266" type="x-p"/> It is a very sad representation which is here made of the state of God's church, of Jacob and Israel, of Zion and Jerusalem; but the emphasis in these verses seems to be laid all along upon the hand of God in the calamities which they were groaning under. The grief is not so much that such and such things are done as that God has done them, that he appears angry with them; it is he that chastens them, and chastens them <hi type="italic">in wrath</hi> and <hi type="italic">in his hot displeasure;</hi> he has become their enemy, and fights against them; and this, this is the wormwood and the gall in the affliction and the misery. <div eID="gen18266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18267" type="x-p"/> I. Time was when God's delight was in his church, and he appeared to her, and appeared for her, as a friend. But now his displeasure is against her; he is angry with her, and appears and acts against her as an enemy. This is frequently repeated here, and sadly lamented. What he has done he has done <hi type="italic">in his anger;</hi> this makes the present day a melancholy day indeed with us, that it is <hi type="italic">the day of his anger</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.1">v. 1</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.2">v. 2</reference>) it is <hi type="italic">in his wrath,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.3">v. 3</reference>) it is <hi type="italic">in his fierce anger,</hi> that he has <hi type="italic">thrown down</hi> and <hi type="italic">cut off,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.6">v. 6</reference>) <hi type="italic">in the indignation of his anger.</hi> Note, To those who know how to value God's favour nothing appears more dreadful than his anger; corrections in love are easily borne, but rebukes in love wound deeply. It is God's wrath that <hi type="italic">burns against Jacob like a flaming fire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.3">v. 3</reference>), and it is a consuming fire; it <hi type="italic">devours round about,</hi> devours all her honours, all her comforts. This is the <hi type="italic">fury that is poured out like fire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.4">v. 4</reference>), like the fire and brimstone which were rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah; but it was their sin that kindled this fire. God is such a tender Father to his children that we may be sure he is never angry with them but when they provoke him, and give him cause to be angry; nor is he ever angry more than there is cause for. God's covenant with them was that if they would <hi type="italic">obey his voice</hi> he would be <hi type="italic">an enemy to their enemies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.22">Exod. xxiii. 22</reference>), and he had been so as long as they kept close to him; but now he is an enemy to them; at least he is <hi type="italic">as an enemy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.5">v. 5</reference>. He has <hi type="italic">bent his bow like an enemy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.4">v. 4</reference>. He stood <hi type="italic">with his right hand</hi> stretched out against them, and a sword drawn in it <hi type="italic">as an adversary.</hi> God is not really an enemy to his people, no, not when he is angry with them and corrects them in anger. We may be sorely displeased against our dearest friends and relations, whom yet we are far from having an enmity to. But sometimes he is <hi type="italic">as an enemy</hi> to them, when all his providences concerning them seem in outward appearance to have a tendency to their ruin, when every thing made against them and nothing for them. But, blessed be God, Christ is <hi type="italic">our peace,</hi> our peacemaker, who has slain the enmity, and in him we may <hi type="italic">agree with our adversary,</hi> which it is our wisdom to do, since it is in vain to contend with him, and he offers us advantageous conditions of peace. <div eID="gen18267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18268" type="x-p"/> II. Time was when God's church appeared very bright, and illustrious, and considerable among the nations; but now <hi type="italic">the Lord has covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.1">v. 1</reference>), a dark cloud, which is very terrible to himself, and through which she cannot see his face; <hi type="italic">a thick cloud</hi> (so that word signifies), a <hi type="italic">black cloud,</hi> which eclipses all her glory and conceals her excellency; not such a cloud as that under which God conducted them through the wilderness, or that in which God took possession of the temple and filled it with his glory: no, that side of the cloud is now turned towards them which was turned towards the Egyptians in the Red Sea. The <hi type="italic">beauty of Israel is now cast down from heaven to the earth;</hi> their princes (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.19">2 Sam. i. 19</reference>), their religious worship, their beauty of holiness, all that which recommended them to the affection and esteem of their neighbours and rendered them amiable, which had <hi type="italic">lifted them up to heaven,</hi> was now withered and gone, because God had covered it with a cloud. He has <hi type="italic">cut off all the horn of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.3">v. 3</reference>), all her beauty and majesty (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">Ps. cxxxii. 17</reference>), all her plenty and fulness, and all her power and authority. They had, in their pride, lifted up their horn against God, and therefore justly will God <hi type="italic">cut off their horn.</hi> He disabled them to resist and oppose their enemies; he <hi type="italic">turned back their right hand,</hi> so that they were not able to follow the blow which they gave nor to ward off the blow which was given them. What can their right hand do against the enemy when God draws it back, and withers it, as he did Jeroboam's? Thus was the <hi type="italic">beauty of Israel cast down,</hi> when a people famed for courage were not able to stand their ground nor make good their post. <div eID="gen18268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18269" type="x-p"/> III. Time was when Jerusalem and the cities of Judah were strong and well fortified, were trusted to by the inhabitants and let alone by the enemy as impregnable. But now the lord has in anger <hi type="italic">swallowed them up;</hi> they are quite gone; the forts and barriers are taken away, and the invaders meet with no opposition: the stately structures, which were their strength and beauty, are pulled down and laid waste. 1. The Lord has in anger <hi type="italic">swallowed up all the habitations of Jacob</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.2">v. 2</reference>), both the cities and the country houses; they are burnt, or otherwise destroyed, so totally ruined that they seem to have been <hi type="italic">swallowed up,</hi> and no remains left of them. He has <hi type="italic">swallowed up, and has not pitied.</hi> One would have thought it a pity that such sumptuous houses, so well built, so well furnished, should be quite destroyed, ad that some pity should have been had for the poor inhabitants that were thus dislodged and driven to wander; but God's wonted compassion seemed to fail: <hi type="italic">He has swallowed up Israel,</hi> as a lion swallows up his prey, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.5">v. 5</reference>. 2. He has <hi type="italic">swallowed up</hi> not only her common habitations, but her palaces, <hi type="italic">all her palaces,</hi> the habitations of their princes and great men (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.5">v. 5</reference>), though those were most stately, and strong, and rich, and well guarded. God's judgments, when they come with commission, level palaces with cottages, and as easily swallow them up. If palaces be polluted with sin, as theirs were, let them expect to be visited with a curse, which shall <hi type="italic">consume them, with the timber thereof and the stones thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.5.4">Zech. v. 4</reference>. 3. He had destroyed not only their dwelling-places, but their <hi type="italic">strong-holds,</hi> their castles, citadels, and places of defence. These he has <hi type="italic">thrown down in his wrath,</hi> and <hi type="italic">brought them to the ground;</hi> for shall they stand in the way of his judgments, and give check to the progress of them? No; let them drop like leaves in autumn; let them be raised to the foundations, and made to touch the <hi type="italic">ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.2">v. 2</reference>. And again (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">He has destroyed his strong-holds;</hi> for what strength could they have against God? And thus he <hi type="italic">increased in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation,</hi> for they could not but be in a dreadful consternation when they saw all their defence departed from them. This is again insisted on, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.7-Lam.2.9">v. 7-9</reference>. In order to the <hi type="italic">swallowing up of her palaces,</hi> he has <hi type="italic">given up into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces,</hi> which were their security, and, when they are <hi type="italic">broken down,</hi> the palaces themselves are soon broken into. The walls of palaces cannot protect them, unless God himself be a wall of fire round about them. This God did <hi type="italic">in his anger,</hi> and yet he has done it deliberately. It is the result of a previous purpose, and is done by a wise and steady providence; for the Lord has <hi type="italic">purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion;</hi> he brought the Chaldean army in on purpose to do this execution. Note, Whatever desolations God makes in his church, they are all according to his counsels; he <hi type="italic">performs the thing that is appointed for us,</hi> even that which makes most against us. But, when it is done, he has <hi type="italic">stretched out a line,</hi> a measuring line, to do it exactly and by measure: hitherto the destruction shall go, and no further; no more shall be cut off than what is marked to be so. Or it is meant of <hi type="italic">the line of confusion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.11">Isa. xxxiv. 11</reference>), a levelling line; for he will go on with his work; he <hi type="italic">has not withdrawn his hand from destroying,</hi> that right hand which he stretched out against his people as <hi type="italic">an adversary,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.4">v. 4</reference>. As far as the purpose went the performance shall go, and his hand shall accomplish his counsel to the utmost, and not be withdrawn. Therefore he made the <hi type="italic">rampart and the wall,</hi> which the people had rejoiced in and upon which perhaps they had <hi type="italic">made merry,</hi> to <hi type="italic">lament,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">languished together;</hi> the <hi type="italic">walls and the ramparts,</hi> or bulwarks, upon them, fell together, and were left to condole with one another on their fall. <hi type="italic">Her gates</hi> are gone in an instant, so that one would think they were sunk into the ground with their own weight, and <hi type="italic">he has destroyed and broken her bars,</hi> those bars of Jerusalem's gates which formerly <hi type="italic">he had strengthened,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.147.13">Ps. cxlvii. 13</reference>. Gates and bars will stand us in no stead when God has withdrawn his protection. <div eID="gen18269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18270" type="x-p"/> IV. Time was when their government flourished, their princes made a figure, their kingdom was great among the nations, and the balance of power was on their side; but now it is quite otherwise: <hi type="italic">He has polluted the kingdom and the princes thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.2">v. 2</reference>. They had first polluted themselves with their idolatries, and then God dealt with them as with polluted things; he threw them to the dunghill, the fittest place for them. He has given up their glory, which was looked upon as sacred (that is a character we give to majesty), to be trampled upon and profaned; and no marvel that the king and the priest, whose characters were always deemed venerable and inviolable, are despised by every body, when God has, <hi type="italic">in the indignation of his anger, despised the king and the priest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.6">v. 6</reference>. He has abandoned them; he looks upon them as no longer worthy of the honours conveyed to them by the covenants of royalty and priesthood, but as having forfeited both; and then Zedekiah the king was used despitefully, and Seraiah the chief priest put to death as a malefactor. The crown has fallen from their heads, for <hi type="italic">her king and her princes are among the Gentiles,</hi> prisoners among them, insulted over by them (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">v. 9</reference>), and treated not only as common persons, but as the basest, without any regard to their character. Note, It is just with God to debase those by his judgments who have by sin debased themselves. <div eID="gen18270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18271" type="x-p"/> V. Time was when the ordinances of God were administered among them in their power and purity, and they had those tokens of God's presence with them; but now those were taken from them, that part of the <hi type="italic">beauty of Israel</hi> was gone which was indeed their greatest beauty. 1. The ark was God's footstool, under the mercy-seat, between the cherubim; this was of all others the most sacred symbol of God's presence (it is called his <hi type="italic">footstool,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1 Chron. xxviii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.99.5">Ps. xcix. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.132.7">cxxxii. 7</reference>); there the Shechinah rested, and with an eye to this Israel was often protected and saved; but now he <hi type="italic">remembered not his footstool.</hi> The ark itself was suffered, as it should seem, to fall into the hands of the Chaldeans. God, being angry, threw that away; for it shall be no longer his footstool; the earth shall be so, as it had been before the ark was, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1">Isa. lxvi. 1</reference>. Of what little value are the tokens of his presence when his presence is gone! Nor was this the first time that God gave his ark into captivity, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.61">Ps. lxxviii. 61</reference>. God and his kingdom can stand without that footstool. 2. Those that ministered in holy things had been <hi type="italic">pleasant to the eye in the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.4">v. 4</reference>); they had been <hi type="italic">purer than snow, whiter than milk</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.7">ch. iv. 7</reference>); none more pleasant in the eyes of all good people than those that did the service of the tabernacle. But now these are slain, and their <hi type="italic">blood is mingled with their sacrifices.</hi> Thus is the priest despised as well as the king. Note, When those that were pleasant to the eye in Zion's tabernacle are slain God must be acknowledged in it; he has done it, and the <hi type="italic">burning which the Lord has kindled must be bewailed</hi> by the whole house of Israel, as in the case of Nadab and Abihu, <reference osisRef="Lev.10.6">Lev. x. 6</reference>. 3. The temple was God's tabernacle (as the tabernacle, while that was in being, was called <hi type="italic">his temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>) and this <hi type="italic">he has violently taken away</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.6">v. 6</reference>); he has plucked up the stakes of it and cut the cords; it shall be no more a tabernacle, much less his; he has <hi type="italic">taken it away,</hi> as the keeper <hi type="italic">of a garden</hi> takes away his shovel or shade, when he has done with it and has no more occasion for it; he takes it down as easily, as speedily, and with a little regret and reluctance as if it were but a <hi type="italic">cottage in a vineyard or a lodge in a garden of cucumbers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Isa. i. 8</reference>), but a <hi type="italic">booth which the keeper makes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.27.18">Job xxvii. 18</reference>. When men profane God's tabernacle it is just with him to take it from them. God has justly refused to <hi type="italic">smell their solemn assemblies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.21">Amos v. 21</reference>); they had provoked him to withdraw from them, and then no marvel that he has <hi type="italic">destroyed his places of the assembly;</hi> what should they do with the places when the services had become an abomination? He has now <hi type="italic">abhorred his sanctuary</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.7">v. 7</reference>); it has been defiled with sin, that only thing which he hates, and for the sake of that he abhors even his sanctuary, which he had delighted in and called <hi type="italic">his rest for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">Ps. cxxxii. 14</reference>. Thus he had <hi type="italic">done to Shiloh.</hi> Now the enemies have made as great <hi type="italic">a noise</hi> of revelling and blaspheming <hi type="italic">in the house of the Lord</hi> as ever had been made with the temple-songs and music <hi type="italic">in the day of a solemn feast,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.4">Ps. lxxiv. 4</reference>. Some, by the <hi type="italic">places of the assembly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.6">v. 6</reference>), understand not only the temple, but the synagogues, and the schools of the prophets, which the enemy had <hi type="italic">burnt up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.8">Ps. lxxiv. 8</reference>. 4. The solemn feasts and the sabbaths had been carefully remembered, and the people constantly put in mind of them; but now the Lord has <hi type="italic">caused those to be forgotten,</hi> not only in the country, among those that lived at a distance, but even in Zion itself; for there were none left to remember them, nor were there the places left where they used to be observed. Now that Zion was in ruins no difference was made between sabbath time and other times; every day was a day of mourning, so that all the <hi type="italic">solemn feasts were forgotten.</hi> Note, It is just with God to deprive those of the benefit and comfort of sabbaths and solemn feasts who have not duly valued them, nor conscientiously observed them, but have profaned them, which was one of the sins that the Jews were often charged with. Those that have <hi type="italic">seen the days of the Son of man,</hi> and slighted them, may <hi type="italic">desire to see one of those days</hi> and not be permitted, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.22">Luke xvii. 22</reference>. 5. The altar that had sanctified their gifts is now cast off, for God will no more accept their gifts, nor be honoured by their sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.7">v. 7</reference>. The altar was <hi type="italic">the table of the Lord,</hi> but God will no longer keep house among them; he will neither feast them nor feast with them. 6. They had been blest with prophets and teachers of the law; but now <hi type="italic">the law is no more</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">v. 9</reference>); it is no more read by the people, no more expounded by the scribes; the tables of the law are gone with the ark; the book of the law is taken from them, and the people are forbidden to have it. What should those do with Bibles who had made no better improvement of them when they had them? <hi type="italic">Her prophets also find no vision from the Lord;</hi> God <hi type="italic">answers them no more by prophets and dreams,</hi> which was the melancholy case of Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">1 Sam. xxviii. 15</reference>. They had persecuted God's prophets, and despised the visions they had from the Lord, and therefore it is just with God to say that they shall have no more prophets, no more visions. Let them go to the prophets that had flattered and deceived them with visions of their own hearts, for they shall have none from God to comfort them, or tell them <hi type="italic">how long.</hi> Those that misuse God's prophets justly lose them.

<div eID="gen18271" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Complicated Sorrows. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18272" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> The elders of the daughter of Zion sit upon the ground, <hi type="italic">and</hi> keep silence: they have cast up dust upon their heads; they have girded themselves with sackcloth: the virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground. <hi type="super">11</hi> Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city. <hi type="super">12</hi> They say to their mothers, Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> corn and wine? when they swooned as the wounded in the streets of the city, when their soul was poured out into their mothers' bosom. <hi type="super">13</hi> What thing shall I take to witness for thee? what thing shall I liken to thee, O daughter of Jerusalem? what shall I equal to thee, that I may comfort thee, O virgin daughter of Zion? for thy breach <hi type="italic">is</hi> great like the sea: who can heal thee? <hi type="super">14</hi> Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee: and they have not discovered thine iniquity, to turn away thy captivity; but have seen for thee false burdens and causes of banishment. <hi type="super">15</hi> All that pass by clap <hi type="italic">their</hi> hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">saying, Is</hi> this the city that <hi type="italic">men</hi> call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth? <hi type="super">16</hi> All thine enemies have opened their mouth against thee: they hiss and gnash the teeth: they say, We have swallowed <hi type="italic">her</hi> up: certainly this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the day that we looked for; we have found, we have seen <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">17</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath done <hi type="italic">that</hi> which he had devised; he hath fulfilled his word that he had commanded in the days of old: he hath thrown down, and hath not pitied: and he hath caused <hi type="italic">thine</hi> enemy to rejoice over thee, he hath set up the horn of thine adversaries. <hi type="super">18</hi> Their heart cried unto the Lord, O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears run down like a river day and night: give thyself no rest; let not the apple of thine eye cease. <hi type="super">19</hi> Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him for the life of thy young children, that faint for hunger in the top of every street. <hi type="super">20</hi> Behold, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and consider to whom thou hast done this. Shall the women eat their fruit, <hi type="italic">and</hi> children of a span long? shall the priest and the prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord? <hi type="super">21</hi> The young and the old lie on the ground in the streets: my virgins and my young men are fallen by the sword; thou hast slain <hi type="italic">them</hi> in the day of thine anger; thou hast killed, <hi type="italic">and</hi> not pitied. <hi type="super">22</hi> Thou hast called as in a solemn day my terrors round about, so that in the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's anger none escaped nor remained: those that I have swaddled and brought up hath mine enemy consumed. <div eID="gen18272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18273" type="x-p"/> Justly are these called <hi type="italic">Lamentations,</hi> and they are very pathetic ones, the expressions of grief in perfection, mourning and woe, and nothing else, like the contents of Ezekiel's roll, <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.10">Ezek. ii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen18273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18274" type="x-p"/> I. Copies of lamentations are here presented and they are painted to the life. 1.
