The judges and magistrates, who used to appear in robes of state, have laid them aside, or rather are stripped of them, and put on the habit of mourners (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.10">v. 10</reference>); the elders now sit no longer in the judgment-seats, the <hi type="italic">thrones of the house of David,</hi> but they <hi type="italic">sit upon the ground,</hi> having no seat to repose themselves in, or in token of great grief, as Job's friends <hi type="italic">sat with him upon the ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.2.13">Job ii. 13</reference>. They open not their mouth in the gate, as usual, to give their opinion, but they <hi type="italic">keep silence,</hi> overwhelmed with grief, and not knowing what to say. They have <hi type="italic">cast dust upon their heads, and girded themselves with sackcloth,</hi> as deep mourners used to do; they had lost their power and wealth, and that made the grieve thus. <hi type="italic">Ploratur lachrymis amissa pecunia veris—Genuine are the tears which we shed over lost property.</hi> 2. The young ladies, who used to dress themselves so richly, and <hi type="italic">walk with stretched-forth necks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Isa. iii. 16</reference>), now are humbled; <hi type="italic">The virgins of Jerusalem hang down their heads to the ground;</hi> those are made to know sorrow who seemed to bid defiance to it and were always disposed to be merry. 3. The prophet himself is a pattern to the mourners, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">v. 11</reference>. His <hi type="italic">eyes do fail with tears;</hi> he has wept till he can weep no more, has almost wept his eyes out, wept himself blind. Nor are the inward impressions of grief short of the outward expressions. <hi type="italic">His bowels are troubled,</hi> as they were when he saw these calamities coming (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.19-Jer.4.20">Jer. iv. 19, 20</reference>), which, one would think, might have excused him now; but even he, to whom they were no surprise, felt them an insupportable grief, to such a degree that his <hi type="italic">liver is poured out on the earth;</hi> he felt himself a perfect colliquation; all his entrails were melted and dissolved, as <reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Ps. xxii. 14</reference>. Jeremiah himself had better treatment than his neighbours, better than he had had before from his own countrymen, nay, their destruction was his deliverance, their captivity his enlargement; the same that made them prisoners made him a favourite; and yet his private interests are swallowed up in a concern for the public, and he bewails the <hi type="italic">destruction of the daughter of his people</hi> as sensibly as if he himself had been the greatest sufferer in that common calamity. Note, The judgments of God upon the land and nation are to be lamented by us, though we, for our parts, may escape pretty well. <div eID="gen18274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18275" type="x-p"/> II. Calls to lamentation are here given: <hi type="italic">The heart of the people cried unto the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.2.18">v. 18</reference>. Some fear it was a cry, not of true repentance, but of bitter complaint; their heart was as full of grief as it could hold, and they gave vent to it in doleful shrieks and outcries, in which they made use of God's name; yet we will charitably suppose that many of them did in sincerity cry unto God for mercy in their distress; and the prophet bids them go on to do so: "<hi type="italic">O wall of the daughter of Zion!</hi> either you that stand upon the wall, you <hi type="italic">watchmen on the walls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Isa. lxii. 6</reference>), when you see the enemies encamped about the walls and making their approaches towards them, or <hi type="italic">because of the wall</hi> (that is the subject of the lamentation), because of the <hi type="italic">breaking down of the wall</hi> (which was not done till about a month after the city was taken), because of this further calamity, let <hi type="italic">the daughter of Zion lament</hi> still." This was a thing which Nehemiah lamented long after, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.3-Neh.1.4">Neh. i. 3, 4</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Let tears run down like a river day and night,</hi> weep without intermission, give thyself no rest from weeping, <hi type="italic">let not the apple of thy eye cease.</hi>" This intimates, 1. That the calamities would be continuing, and the causes of grief would frequently recur, and fresh occasion would be given them every day and every night to bemoan themselves. 2. That they would be apt, by degrees, to grow insensible and stupid under the hand of God, and would need to be still called upon to afflict their souls yet more and more, till their proud and hard hearts were thoroughly humbled and softened. <div eID="gen18275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18276" type="x-p"/> III. Causes for lamentation are here assigned, and the calamities that are to be bewailed are very particularly and pathetically described. <div eID="gen18276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18277" type="x-p"/> 1. Multitudes perish by famine, a very sore judgment, and piteous is the case of those that fall under it. God had corrected them by scarcity of provisions through want of rain some time before (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.1">Jer. xiv. 1</reference>), and they were not brought to repentance by that lower degree of this judgment, and therefore now by the straitness of the siege God brought it upon them in extremity; for, (1.) The children died for hunger in their mothers' arms: <hi type="italic">The children and sucklings,</hi> whose innocent and helpless state entitles them to relief as soon as any, <hi type="italic">swoon in the streets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">v. 11</reference>) <hi type="italic">as the wounded</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.12">v. 12</reference>), there being no food to be had for them; those that are starved die as surely as those that are stabbed. They lie a great while crying to their poor mothers for corn to feed them and wine to refresh them, for they are such as had been bred up to the use of wine and wanted it now; but there is none for them, so that at length <hi type="italic">their soul is poured into their mothers' bosom,</hi> and there they breathe their last. This is mentioned again (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">They faint for hunger in the top of every street.</hi> Yet this is not the worst, (2.) There were some little children that were slain by their mothers' hands and eaten, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">v. 20</reference>. Such was the scarcity of provision that the <hi type="italic">women ate the fruit</hi> of their own bodies, even their children when they were but of <hi type="italic">a span long,</hi> according to the threatening, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">Deut. xxviii. 53</reference>. The like was done in the siege of Samaria, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.29">2 Kings vi. 29</reference>. Such extremities, nay, such barbarities, were they brought to by the famine. Let us, in our abundance, thank God that we have food convenient, not only for ourselves, but for our children. <div eID="gen18277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18278" type="x-p"/> 2. Multitudes fall by the sword, which devours one as well as another, especially when it is in the hand of such cruel enemies as the Chaldeans were. (1.) They spared no character, no, not the most distinguished; even the <hi type="italic">priest and the prophet,</hi> who of all men, one would think, might expect protection from heaven and veneration on earth, <hi type="italic">are slain,</hi> not abroad in the field of battle, where they are out of their place, as Hophni and Phinehas, but in <hi type="italic">the sanctuary of the Lord,</hi> the place of their business and which they hoped would be a refuge to them. (2.) They spared no age, no, not those who, by reason of their tender or their decrepit age, were exempted from taking up the sword; for even they <hi type="italic">perished by the sword.</hi> "The young, who have not yet come to bear arms, and the old, who have had their <hi type="italic">discharge, lie on the ground, slain in the streets,</hi> till some kind hand is found that will bury them." (3.) They spared no sex: <hi type="italic">My virgins and my young men have fallen by the sword.</hi> In the most barbarous military executions that ever we read of the virgins were spared, and made part of the spoil (<reference osisRef="Num.31.18">Num. xxxi. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.30">Judges v. 30</reference>), but here the virgins were put to the sword, as well as the young men. (4.) This was the <hi type="italic">Lord's doing;</hi> he suffered the sword of the Chaldeans to devour thus without distinction: <hi type="italic">Thou has slain them in the day of thy anger,</hi> for it is God that <hi type="italic">kills and makes alive,</hi> and saves alive, as he pleases. But that which follows is very harsh: <hi type="italic">Thou has killed, and not pitied;</hi> for his soul is <hi type="italic">grieved for the misery of Israel.</hi> The enemies that used them thus cruelly were such as he had both mustered and summoned (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast called in, as in a solemn day, my terrors round about,</hi> that is, the Chaldeans, who are such a terror to me;" enemies crowded into Jerusalem now as thickly as ever worshippers used to do on a solemn festival, so that they were quite overpowered with numbers, and none escaped nor remained; Jerusalem was made a perfect slaughter-house. Mothers are cut to the heart to see those whom they have taken such care of, and pains with, and whom they have been so tender of, thus inhumanly used, suddenly cut off, though not soon reared: <hi type="italic">Those that I have swaddled, and brought up, has my enemy consumed,</hi> as if they were brought forth for the murderer, like lambs for the butcher, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.13">Hosea ix. 13</reference>. Zion, who was a mother to them all, lamented to see those who were brought up in her courts, and under the tuition of her oracles, thus made a prey. <div eID="gen18278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18279" type="x-p"/> 3. Their false prophets cheated them, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.14">v. 14</reference>. This was a thing which Jeremiah had lamented long before, and had observed with a great concern (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.13">Jer. xiv. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ah! Lord God, the prophets say unto them, You shall not see the sword;</hi> and here he inserts it among his lamentations: <hi type="italic">Thy prophets have seen vain and foolish things for thee;</hi> they pretended to discover for thee, and then to discover to thee, the mind and will of God, to see <hi type="italic">the visions of the Almighty</hi> and then to speak his words; but they were all vain and foolish things; their visions were all their own fancies, and, if they thought they had any, it was only the product of a crazed head or a heated imagination, as appeared by what they delivered, which was all idle and impertinent: nay, it is most likely that they themselves knew that the visions they pretended were counterfeit, and all a sham, and made use of only to colour that which they designedly imposed upon the people with, that they might make an interest in them for themselves. They are thy prophets, not God's prophets; he never sent them, nor were they pastors after his heart, but the people set them up, told them what they should say, so that they were <hi type="italic">prophets after their hearts.</hi> (1.) Prophets should tell people of their faults, should show them their sins, that they may bring them to repentance, and so prevent their ruin; but these prophets knew that would lose them the people's affections and contributions, and knew they could not reprove their hearers without reproaching themselves at the same time, and therefore <hi type="italic">they have not discovered thy iniquity;</hi> they saw it not themselves, or, if they did, saw so little evil in it, or danger from it, that they would not tell them of it, though that might have been a means, by taking away their iniquity, to turn away their captivity. (2.) Prophets should warn people of the judgments of God coming upon them, but these <hi type="italic">saw for them false burdens;</hi> the messages they pretended to deliver to them from God they knew to be false, and falsely ascribed to God; so that, by soothing them up in carnal security, they caused that banishment which, by plain dealing, they might have prevented. <div eID="gen18279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18280" type="x-p"/> 4. Their neighbours laughed at them (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that pass by thee clap their hands at thee.</hi> Jerusalem had made a great figure, got a great name, and borne a great sway, among the nations; it was the envy and terror of all about; and, when the city was thus reduced; they all (as men are apt to do in such a case) triumphed in its fall; <hi type="italic">they hissed, and wagged the head,</hi> pleasing themselves to see how much it had fallen from its former pretensions. <hi type="italic">Is this the city</hi> (said they) <hi type="italic">that men called the perfection of beauty?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">Ps. l. 2</reference>. How is it now the perfection of deformity! Where is all its beauty now? <hi type="italic">Is this the city which was called the joy of the whole earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Ps. xlviii. 2</reference>), which rejoiced in the gifts of God's bounty and grace more than any other place, and which all the earth rejoiced in? Where is all its joy now and all its glorying? It is a great sin thus to make a jest of others' miseries, and adds very much affliction to the afflicted. <div eID="gen18280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18281" type="x-p"/> 5. Their enemies triumphed over them, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">v. 16</reference>. Those that wished ill to Jerusalem and her peace now vent their spite and malice, which before they concealed; they now <hi type="italic">open their mouths,</hi> nay, they widen them; they <hi type="italic">hiss and gnash their teeth</hi> in scorn and indignation; they triumph in their own success against her, and the rich prey they have got in making themselves masters of Jerusalem: "<hi type="italic">We have swallowed her up;</hi> it is our doing, and it is our gain; it is all our own now. Jerusalem shall never be either courted or feared as she has been. <hi type="italic">Certainly this is the day that we have long looked for; we have found it; we have seen it; aha! so would we have it.</hi>" Note, The enemies of the church are apt to take its shocks for its ruins, and to triumph in them accordingly; but they will find themselves deceived; <hi type="italic">for the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church.</hi> <div eID="gen18281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18282" type="x-p"/> 6. Their God, in all this, appeared against them (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has done that which he had devised.</hi> The destroyers of Jerusalem could have <hi type="italic">no power against her unless it were given them from above.</hi> They are but the sword in God's hand; it is he that has <hi type="italic">thrown down, and has not pitied.</hi> "In this controversy of his with us we have not had the usual instances of his compassion towards us." <hi type="italic">He has caused thy enemy to rejoice over thee</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Job.30.11">Job xxx. 11</reference>); <hi type="italic">he has set up the horn of thy adversaries,</hi> has given them power and matter for pride. This is indeed the highest aggravation of the trouble, that God has become their enemy, and yet it is the strongest argument for patience under it; we are bound to submit to what God does, for, (1.) It is the performance of his purpose: <hi type="italic">The Lord has done that which he had devised;</hi> it is done with counsel and deliberation, not rashly, or upon a sudden resolve; it is the <hi type="italic">evil that he has framed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">Jer. xviii. 11</reference>), and we may be sure it is framed so as exactly to answer the intention. What God devises against his people is designed for them, and so it will be found in the issue. (2.) It is the accomplishment of his predictions; it is the fulfilling of the scripture; he has now <hi type="italic">put in execution his word that he had commanded in the days of old.</hi> When he gave them his law by Moses he told them what judgments he would certainly inflict upon them if they transgressed that law; and now that they have been guilty of the transgression of this law he had executed the sentence of it, according to <reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Lev. xxvi. 16,</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.15">Deut. xxviii. 15</reference>. Note, In all the providences of God concerning his church it is good to take notice of the fulfilling of his word; for there is an exact agreement between the judgments of God's hand and the judgments of his mouth, and when they are compared they will mutually explain and illustrate each other. <div eID="gen18282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18283" type="x-p"/> IV. Comforts for the cure of these lamentations are here sought for and prescribed. <div eID="gen18283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18284" type="x-p"/> 1. They are sought for and enquired after, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.13">v. 13</reference>. The prophet seeks to find out some suitable acceptable words to say to her in this case: <hi type="italic">Wherewith shall I comfort thee, O virgin! daughter of Zion?</hi> Note, We should endeavour to comfort those whose calamities we lament, and, when our passions have made the worst of them, our wisdom should correct them and labour to make the best of them; we should study to make our sympathies with our afflicted friends turn to their consolation. Now the two most common topics of comfort, in case of affliction, are here tried, but are laid by because they would not hold. We commonly endeavour to comfort our friends by telling them, (1.) That their case is not singular, nor without precedent; there are many whose trouble is greater, and lies heavier upon them, than theirs does; but Jerusalem's case will not admit this argument: "<hi type="italic">What thing shall I liken to thee,</hi> or <hi type="italic">what shall I equal to thee, that I may comfort thee?</hi> What city, what country, is there, whose case is parallel to thine? What witness shall I produce to prove an example that will reach thy present calamitous state? Alas! there is none, no sorrow like thine, because there is none whose honour was like thine." (2.) We tell them that their case is not desperate, but that it may easily be remedied; but neither will that be admitted here, upon a view of human probabilities; for <hi type="italic">thy breach is great, like the sea,</hi> like the breach which the sea sometimes makes upon the land, which cannot be repaired, but still grows wider and wider. Thou art wounded, and <hi type="italic">who shall heal thee?</hi> No wisdom nor power of man can repair the desolations of such a broken shattered state. It is to no purpose therefore to administer any of these common cordials; therefore, <div eID="gen18284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18285" type="x-p"/> 2. The method of cure prescribed is to address themselves to God, and by a penitent prayer to commit their case to him, and to be instant and constant in such prayers (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Arise</hi> out of thy dust, out of thy despondency, <hi type="italic">cry out in the night,</hi> watch unto prayer; when others are asleep, be thou upon thy knees, importunate with God for mercy; <hi type="italic">in the beginning of the watches,</hi> of each of the four watches, of the night (let thy <hi type="italic">eyes prevent</hi> them, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.148">Ps. cxix. 148</reference>), then <hi type="italic">pour out thy heart like water before the Lord,</hi> be free and full in prayer, be sincere and serious in prayer, open thy mind, spread thy case before the Lord; <hi type="italic">lift up thy hands towards him</hi> in holy desire and expectation; beg for <hi type="italic">the life of thy young children.</hi> These poor lambs, what have they done? <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.17">2 Sam. xxiv. 17</reference>. Take with you words, take with you these words (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">Behold, O Lord! and consider to whom thou hast done this,</hi> with whom thou hast dealt thus. Are they not thy own, the seed of Abraham thy friend and of Jacob thy chosen? Lord, take their case into thy compassionate consideration!" Note, Prayer is a salve for every sore, even the sorest, a remedy for every malady, even the most grievous. And our business in prayer is not to prescribe, but to subscribe to the wisdom and will of God; to refer our case to him, and then to leave it with him. <hi type="italic">Lord, behold and consider,</hi> and <hi type="italic">thy will be done.</hi>  <chapter eID="Lam.2"/> <div eID="gen18285" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen18288" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18287" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet's Personal Affliction. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18289" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the man <hi type="italic">that</hi> hath seen affliction by the rod of his wrath. <hi type="super">2</hi> He hath led me, and brought <hi type="italic">me into</hi> darkness, but not <hi type="italic">into</hi> light. <hi type="super">3</hi> Surely against me is he turned; he turneth his hand <hi type="italic">against me</hi> all the day. <hi type="super">4</hi> My flesh and my skin hath he made old; he hath broken my bones. <hi type="super">5</hi> He hath builded against me, and compassed <hi type="italic">me</hi> with gall and travail. <hi type="super">6</hi> He hath set me in dark places, as <hi type="italic">they that be</hi> dead of old. <hi type="super">7</hi> He hath hedged me about, that I cannot get out: he hath made my chain heavy. <hi type="super">8</hi> Also when I cry and shout, he shutteth out my prayer. <hi type="super">9</hi> He hath inclosed my ways with hewn stone, he hath made my paths crooked. <hi type="super">10</hi> He <hi type="italic">was</hi> unto me <hi type="italic">as</hi> a bear lying in wait, <hi type="italic">and as</hi> a lion in secret places. <hi type="super">11</hi> He hath turned aside my ways, and pulled me in pieces: he hath made me desolate. <hi type="super">12</hi> He hath bent his bow, and set me as a mark for the arrow. <hi type="super">13</hi> He hath caused the arrows of his quiver to enter into my reins. <hi type="super">14</hi> I was a derision to all my people; <hi type="italic">and</hi> their song all the day. <hi type="super">15</hi> He hath filled me with bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood. <hi type="super">16</hi> He hath also broken my teeth with gravel stones, he hath covered me with ashes. <hi type="super">17</hi> And thou hast removed my soul far off from peace: I forgat prosperity. <hi type="super">18</hi> And I said, My strength and my hope is perished from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">19</hi> Remembering mine affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the gall. <hi type="super">20</hi> My soul hath <hi type="italic">them</hi> still in remembrance, and is humbled in me. <div eID="gen18289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18290" type="x-p"/> The title of the <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1-Ps.102.28">102nd Psalm</reference> might very fitly be prefixed to this chapter—<hi type="italic">The prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed, and pours out his complaint before the Lord;</hi> for it is very feelingly and fluently that the complaint is here poured out. Let us observe the particulars of it. The prophet complains, 1. That God is angry. This gives both birth and bitterness to the affliction (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am the man,</hi> the remarkable man, <hi type="italic">that has seen affliction,</hi> and has felt it sensibly, <hi type="italic">by the rod of his wrath.</hi> Note, God is sometimes angry with his own people; yet it is to be complained of, not as a sword to cut off, by only as a rod to correct; it is to them <hi type="italic">the rod of his wrath,</hi> a chastening which, though grievous for the present, will in the issue be advantageous. By this rod we must expect to <hi type="italic">see affliction,</hi> and, if we be made to see more than ordinary affliction by that rod, we must not quarrel, for we are sure that the anger is just and affliction mild and mixed with mercy. 2. That he is at a loss and altogether in the dark. Darkness is put for great trouble and perplexity, the want both of comfort and of direction; this was the case of the complainant (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He has led me</hi> by his providence, and an unaccountable chain of events, <hi type="italic">into darkness and not into light,</hi> the darkness I feared and not into the light I hoped for." And (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">He has set me in dark places,</hi> dark as the grave, <hi type="italic">like those that are dead of old,</hi> that are quite forgotten, nobody knows who or what they were. Note, The Israel of God, though children of light, sometimes <hi type="italic">walk in darkness.</hi> 3. That God appears against him as an enemy, as a professed enemy. God had been for him, but no "<hi type="italic">Surely against me is he turned</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.3">v. 3</reference>), as far as I can discern; for <hi type="italic">his hand is turned against me all the day. I am chastened every morning,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.73.14">Ps. lxxiii. 14</reference>. And, when God's hand is continually turned against us, we are tempted to think that his heart is turned against us too. God had said once (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Hos. v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will be as a lion to the house of Judah,</hi> and now he has made his word good (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He was unto me as a bear lying in wait,</hi> surprising me with his judgments, <hi type="italic">and as a lion in secret places;</hi> so that which way soever I went I was in continual fear of being set upon and could never think myself safe." Do men shoot at those thy are enemies to? <hi type="italic">He has bent his bow,</hi> the bow that was ordained against the church's prosecutors, that is bent against her sons, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.12">v. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">He has set me as a mark for his arrow,</hi> which he aims at, and will be sure to hit, and then <hi type="italic">the arrows of his quiver enter into my reins,</hi> give me a mortal wound, an inward wound, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.13">v. 13</reference>. Note, God has many arrows in his quiver, and they fly swiftly and pierce deeply. 4. That he is as one sorely afflicted both in body and mind. The Jewish state may now be fitly compared to a man wrinkled with age, for which there is no remedy (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My flesh and my skin has he made old;</hi> they are wasted and withered, and I look like one that is ready to drop into the grave; nay, <hi type="italic">he has broken my bones,</hi> and so disabled me to help myself, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.15">v. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">He has filled me with bitterness,</hi> a bitter sense of his calamities." God has access to the spirit, and can so embitter that as thereby to embitter all the enjoyments; as, when the stomach is foul, whatever is eaten sours in it: "<hi type="italic">He has made me drunk with wormwood,</hi> so intoxicated me with the sense of my afflictions that I know not what to say or do. <hi type="italic">He has</hi> mingled <hi type="italic">gravel</hi> with my bread, so that <hi type="italic">my teeth</hi> are <hi type="italic">broken</hi> with it (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.16">v. 16</reference>) and what I eat is neither pleasant nor nourishing. <hi type="italic">He has covered me with ashes,</hi> as mourners used to be, or (as some read it) <hi type="italic">he has fed me with ashes. I have eaten ashes like bread,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.102.9">Ps. cii. 9</reference>. 5. That he is not able to discern any way of escape or deliverance (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He has built against me,</hi> as forts and batteries are built against a besieged city. Where there was a way open it is now quite made up: <hi type="italic">He has compassed me</hi> on ever side <hi type="italic">with gall and travel;</hi> I vex, and fret, and tire myself, to find a way of escape, but can find none, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">He has hedged me about, that I cannot get out.</hi>" When Jerusalem was besieged it was said to be <hi type="italic">compassed in on every side,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.43">Luke xix. 43</reference>. "I am chained; and as some notorious malefactors are double-fettered, and loaded with irons, so he <hi type="italic">has made my chain heavy. He has</hi> also (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.9">v. 9</reference>) <hi type="italic">enclosed my ways with hewn stone,</hi> not only hedged up my way <hi type="italic">with thorns</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.6">Hos. ii. 6</reference>), but stopped it up with a stone wall, which cannot be broken through, so that <hi type="italic">my paths are made crooked;</hi> I traverse to and fro, to the right hand, to the left, to try to get forward, but am still turned back." It is just with God to make those who walk in the crooked paths of sin, crossing God's laws, walk in the crooked paths of affliction, crossing their designs and breaking their measures. So (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.11">v. 11</reference>), "<hi type="italic">He has turned aside my ways;</hi> he has blasted all my counsels, ruined my projects, so that I am necessitated to yield to my own ruin. He has <hi type="italic">pulled me in pieces;</hi> he has torn and is gone away (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.14">Hos. v. 14</reference>), and has <hi type="italic">made me desolate,</hi> has deprived me of all society and all comfort in my own soul." 6. That God turns a deaf ear to his prayers (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When I cry and shout,</hi> as one in earnest, as one that would make him hear, yet he <hi type="italic">shuts out my prayer</hi> and will not suffer it to have access to him." God's ear is wont to be open to the prayers of his people, and his door of mercy to those that knock at it; but now both are shut, even to one that <hi type="italic">cries and shouts.</hi> Thus sometimes God seems to be angry even against <hi type="italic">the prayers of his people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.4">Ps. lxxx. 4</reference>), and their case is deplorable indeed when they are denied not only the benefit of an answer, but the comfort of acceptance. 7. That his neighbours make a laughing matter of his troubles (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was a derision to all my people,</hi> to all the wicked among them, who made themselves an one another merry with the public judgments, and particularly the prophet Jeremiah's griefs. I am their song, their <hi type="italic">neginath,</hi> or hand-instrument of music, their <hi type="italic">tabret</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.17.6">Job xvii. 6</reference>), that they play upon, as Nero on his harp when Rome was on fire. 8. That he was ready to despair of relief and deliverance: "Thou hast not only taken peace from me, but hast <hi type="italic">removed my soul far off from peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.17">v. 17</reference>), so that it is not only not within reach, but not within view. <hi type="italic">I forget prosperity;</hi> it is so long since I had it, and so unlikely that I should ever recover it, that I have lost the idea of it. I have been so inured to sorrow and servitude that I know not what joy and liberty mean. I have even given up all for gone, concluding, <hi type="italic">My strength and my hope have perished from the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.18">v. 18</reference>); I can no longer stay myself upon God as my support, for I do not find that he gives me encouragement to do so; nor can I look for his appearing in my behalf, so as to put an end to my troubles, for the case seems remediless, and even my God inexorable." Without doubt it was his infirmity to say this (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.10">Ps. lxxvii. 10</reference>), for with God there is <hi type="italic">everlasting strength,</hi> and he is his people's never-failing hope, whatever they may think. 9. That grief returned upon every remembrance of his troubles, and his reflections were as melancholy as his prospects, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.19-Lam.3.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. Did he endeavour as Job did (<reference osisRef="Job.9.27">Job ix. 27</reference>), to <hi type="italic">forget his complaint?</hi> Alas! it was to no purpose; he remembers, upon all occasions, <hi type="italic">the affliction and the misery, the wormwood and the gall.</hi> Thus emphatically does he speak of his affliction, for thus did he think of it, thus heavily did it lie when he reviewed it! It was an affliction that was misery itself. <hi type="italic">My affliction and my transgression</hi> (so some read it), my trouble and my sin that brought it upon me; this was <hi type="italic">the wormwood and the gall</hi> in <hi type="italic">the affliction and the misery.</hi> It is sin that makes the cup of affliction a bitter cup. <hi type="italic">My soul has them still in remembrance.</hi> The captives in Babylon had all the miseries of the siege in their mind continually and the flames and ruins of Jerusalem still before their eyes, and <hi type="italic">wept when</hi> they <hi type="italic">remembered Zion;</hi> nay, they could <hi type="italic">never forget Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.137.1">Ps. cxxxvii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.5">5</reference>. <hi type="italic">My soul,</hi> having <hi type="italic">them in remembrance, is humbled in me,</hi> not only oppressed with a sense of the trouble, but in bitterness for sin. Note, It becomes us to have humble hearts under humbling providences, and to renew our penitent humiliations for sin upon every remembrance of our afflictions and miseries. Thus we may get good by former corrections and prevent further.

<div eID="gen18290" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Words of Comfort to Israel; The Benefit of Afflictions; Comfort to the Afflicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  588.)</title> <div sID="gen18291" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. <hi type="super">22</hi> <hi type="italic">It is of</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. <hi type="super">23</hi> <hi type="italic">They are</hi> new every morning: great <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy faithfulness. <hi type="super">24</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> my portion, saith my soul; therefore will I hope in him. <hi type="super">25</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> good unto them that wait for him, to the soul <hi type="italic">that</hi> seeketh him. <hi type="super">26</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> good that <hi type="italic">a man</hi> should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> .   27 <hi type="italic">It is</hi> good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth. <hi type="super">28</hi> He sitteth alone and keepeth silence, because he hath borne <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon him. <hi type="super">29</hi> He putteth his mouth in the dust; if so be there may be hope. <hi type="super">30</hi> He giveth <hi type="italic">his</hi> cheek to him that smiteth him: he is filled full with reproach. <hi type="super">31</hi> For the Lord will not cast off for ever: <hi type="super">32</hi> But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. <hi type="super">33</hi> For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men. <hi type="super">34</hi> To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the earth, <hi type="super">35</hi> To turn aside the right of a man before the face of the most High, <hi type="super">36</hi> To subvert a man in his cause, the Lord approveth not. <div eID="gen18291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18292" type="x-p"/> Here the clouds begin to disperse and the sky to clear up; the complaint was very melancholy in the former part of the chapter, and yet here the tune is altered and the mourners in Zion begin to look a little pleasant. But for hope, the heart would break. To save the heart from being quite broken, here is something <hi type="italic">called to mind,</hi> which gives ground for <hi type="italic">hope</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.21">v. 21</reference>), which refers to what comes after, not to what goes before. <hi type="italic">I make to return to my heart</hi> (so the margin words it); what we have had in our hearts, and have laid to our hearts, is sometimes as if it were quite lost and forgotten, till God by his grace make it return to our hearts, that it may be ready to us when we have occasion to use it. "<hi type="italic">I recall</hi> it <hi type="italic">to mind; therefore have I hope,</hi> and am kept from downright despair." Let us see what these things are which he calls to mind. <div eID="gen18292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18293" type="x-p"/> I. That, bad as things are, it is owing to the mercy of God that they are not worse. We are <hi type="italic">afflicted by the rod of his wrath,</hi> but <hi type="italic">it is of the lord's mercies that we are not consumed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.22">v. 22</reference>. When we are in distress we should, for the encouragement of our faith and hope, observe what makes for us as well as what makes against us. Things are bad but they might have been worse, and therefore there is hope that they may be better. Observe here, 1. The streams of mercy acknowledged: <hi type="italic">We are not consumed.</hi> Note, The church of God is like Moses's bush, burning, yet <hi type="italic">not consumed;</hi> whatever hardships it has met with, or may meet with, it shall have a being in the world to the end of time. It is <hi type="italic">persecuted</hi> of men, <hi type="italic">but not forsaken</hi> of God, and therefore, though it is <hi type="italic">cast down,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">not destroyed</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">2 Cor. iv. 9</reference>), corrected, yet <hi type="italic">not consumed,</hi> refined in the furnace as silver, but <hi type="italic">not consumed</hi> as dross. 2. These streams followed up to the fountain: <hi type="italic">It is of the Lord's mercies.</hi> here are mercies in the plural number, denoting the abundance and variety of those mercies. God is an inexhaustible <hi type="italic">fountain of mercy, the Father of mercies.</hi> Note, We all owe it to the sparing mercy of God <hi type="italic">that we are not consumed.</hi> Others have been consumed round about us, and we ourselves have been in the consuming, and yet <hi type="italic">we are not consumed;</hi> we are out of the grave; we are out of hell. Had we been dealt with <hi type="italic">according to our sins,</hi> we should have been consumed long ago; but we have been dealt with <hi type="italic">according to God's mercies,</hi> and we are bound to acknowledge it to his praise. <div eID="gen18293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18294" type="x-p"/> II. That even in the depth of their affliction they still have experience of the tenderness of the divine pity and the truth of the divine promise. They had several times complained that God had not pitied (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.17">ch. ii. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.21">21</reference>), but here they correct themselves, and own, 1. That <hi type="italic">God's compassions fail not;</hi> they do not really fail, no, not even when in anger he seems to have <hi type="italic">shut up his tender mercies.</hi> These rivers of mercy run fully and constantly, but never run dry. No; <hi type="italic">they are new every morning;</hi> every morning we have fresh instances of God's compassion towards us; he visits us with them <hi type="italic">every morning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.7.18">Job vii. 18</reference>); <hi type="italic">every morning does he bring his judgment to light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.5">Zeph. iii. 5</reference>. When our comforts fail, yet God's compassions do not. 2. That <hi type="italic">great is his faithfulness.</hi> Though the covenant seemed to be broken, they owned that it still continued in full force; and, though Jerusalem be in ruins, <hi type="italic">the truth of the Lord endures for ever.</hi> Note, Whatever hard things we suffer, we must never entertain any hard thoughts of God, but must still be ready to own that he is both kind and faithful. <div eID="gen18294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18295" type="x-p"/> III. That God is, and ever will be, the all-sufficient happiness of his people, and they have chosen him and depend upon him to be such (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord is my portion, saith my soul;</hi> that is, 1. "When I have lost all I have in the world, liberty, and livelihood, and almost life itself, yet I have not lost my interest in God." Portions on earth are perishing things, but God is <hi type="italic">portion for ever.</hi> 2. "While I have an interest in God, therein I have enough; I have that which is sufficient to counterbalance all my troubles and make up all my losses." Whatever we are robbed of our portion is safe. 3. "This is that which I depend upon and rest satisfied with: <hi type="italic">Therefore will I hope in him.</hi> I will stay myself upon him, and encourage myself in him, when all other supports and encouragements fail me." Note, It is our duty to make God the portion of our souls, and then to make use of him as our portion and to take the comfort of it in the midst of our lamentations. <div eID="gen18295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18296" type="x-p"/> IV. That those who deal with God will find it is not in vain to trust in him; for, 1. He is good to those who do so, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.25">v. 25</reference>. He is good to all; <hi type="italic">his tender mercies are over all his works;</hi> all his creatures taste of his goodness. But he is in a particular manner <hi type="italic">good to those that wait for him, to the soul that seeks him.</hi> Note, While trouble is prolonged, and deliverance is deferred, we must patiently wait for God and his gracious returns to us. While we <hi type="italic">wait for him</hi> by faith, we must <hi type="italic">seek him</hi> by prayer: our <hi type="italic">souls</hi> must <hi type="italic">seek him,</hi> else we do not seek so as to find. Our seeking will help to keep up our waiting. And to those who thus wait and seek God will be gracious; he will show them his <hi type="italic">marvellous lovingkindness.</hi> 2. Those that do so will find it good for them (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">It is good</hi> (it is our duty, and will be our unspeakable comfort and satisfaction) <hi type="italic">to hope and quietly to wait for the salvation of the Lord,</hi> to hope that it will come, thought the difficulties that lie in the way of it seem insupportable, to wait till it does come, though it be long delayed, and while we wait to be quiet and silent, not quarrelling with God nor making ourselves uneasy, but acquiescing in the divine disposals. <hi type="italic">Father, thy will be done.</hi> If we call this to mind, we may have hope that all will end well at last. <div eID="gen18296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18297" type="x-p"/> V. That afflictions are really good for us, and, if we bear them aright, will work very much for our good. It is not only good to hope and wait for the salvation, but it is good to be under the trouble in the mean time (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.</hi> Many of the young men were carried into captivity. To make them easy in it, he tells them that it was good for them to <hi type="italic">bear the yoke</hi> of that captivity, and they would find it so if they would but accommodate themselves to their condition, and labour to answer God's ends in laying that heavy yoke upon them. It is very applicable to the yoke of God's commands. It is good for young people to take that yoke upon them in their youth; we cannot begin too soon to be religious. It will make our duty the more acceptable to God, and easy to ourselves, if we engage in it when we are young. But here it seems to be meant of the yoke of affliction. Many have found it good to bear this in youth; it has made those humble and serious, and has weaned them from the world, who otherwise would have been proud and unruly, and <hi type="italic">as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke.</hi> But when do we <hi type="italic">bear the yoke</hi> so that it is really <hi type="italic">good for us to bear it in our youth?</hi> He answers in the following verses, 1. When we are sedate and quiet under our afflictions, when we <hi type="italic">sit alone and keep silence,</hi> do not run to and fro into all companies with our complaints, aggravating our calamities, and quarrelling with the disposals of Providence concerning us, but retire into privacy, that we may <hi type="italic">in a day of adversity consider, sit alone,</hi> that we may converse with God and <hi type="italic">commune with our own hearts,</hi> silencing all discontented distrustful thoughts, and laying our hand upon our mouth, as Aaron, who, under a very severe trial, held his peace. We must keep silence under the yoke as those that have borne it upon us, not wilfully pulled it upon our own necks, but patiently submitted to it when God laid it upon us. When those who are afflicted in their youth accommodate themselves to their afflictions, fit their necks to the yoke and study to answer God's end in afflicting them, then they will find it good for them to bear it, for it yields <hi type="italic">the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who are</hi> thus <hi type="italic">exercised thereby.</hi> 2. When we are humble and patient under our affliction. <hi type="italic">He</hi> gets good by the yoke who <hi type="italic">puts his mouth in the dust,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">lays his hand upon his mouth,</hi> in token of submission to the will of God in the affliction, but <hi type="italic">puts it in the dust,</hi> in token of sorrow, and shame, and self-loathing, at the remembrance of sin, and as one perfectly reduced and reclaimed, and brought as those that are vanquished to <hi type="italic">lick the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.9">Ps. lxxii. 9</reference>. And we must thus humble ourselves, <hi type="italic">if so be there may be hope,</hi> or (as it is in the original) <hi type="italic">peradventure there is hope.</hi> If there be any way to acquire and secure a good hope under our afflictions, it is this way, and yet we must be very modest in our expectations of it, must look for it with an <hi type="italic">it may be,</hi> as those who own ourselves utterly unworthy of it. Note, Those who are truly humbled for sin will be glad to obtain a good hope, through grace, upon any terms, though they <hi type="italic">put their mouth in the dust</hi> for it; and those who would have hope must do so, and ascribe it to free grace if they have any encouragements, which may keep their hearts from sinking into the dust when they put their mouth there. 3. When we are meek and mild towards those who are the instruments of our trouble, and are of a forgiving spirit, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.30">v. 30</reference>. <hi type="italic">He</hi> gets good by the yoke who <hi type="italic">gives his cheek to him that smites him,</hi> and rather <hi type="italic">turns the other cheek</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.39">Matt. v. 39</reference>) than returns the second blow. Our Lord Jesus has left us an example of this, for he <hi type="italic">gave his back to the smiter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Isa. l. 6</reference>. He who can bear contempt and reproach, and not <hi type="italic">render railing for railing,</hi> and bitterness for bitterness, who, when he is <hi type="italic">filled full with reproach,</hi> keeps it to himself, and does not retort it and empty it again upon those who filled him with it, but <hi type="italic">pours it out before the Lord</hi> (as those did, <reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Ps. cxxiii. 4</reference>, whose <hi type="italic">souls were exceedingly filled with the contempt of the proud</hi>), he shall find that <hi type="italic">it is good to bear the yoke,</hi> that it shall turn to his spiritual advantage. The sum is, <hi type="italic">If tribulation work patience,</hi> that <hi type="italic">patience</hi> will work <hi type="italic">experience,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">experience a hope that makes not ashamed.</hi> <div eID="gen18297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18298" type="x-p"/> VI. That God will graciously return to his people with seasonable comforts <hi type="italic">according to the time that he has afflicted them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.31-Lam.3.32">v. 31, 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> the sufferer is thus penitent, thus patient, because he believes that God is gracious and merciful, which is the great inducement both to evangelical repentance and to Christian patience. We may bear ourselves up with this, 1. That, when we are cast down, yet we are not cast off; the father's correcting his son is not a disinheriting of him. 2. That though we may seem to be cast off for a time, while sensible comforts are suspended and desired salvations deferred, yet we are not really cast off, because not <hi type="italic">cast off for ever;</hi> the controversy with us shall not be perpetual. 3. That, whatever sorrow we are in, it is what God has allotted us, and his hand is in it. It is he that causes grief, and therefore we may be assured it is ordered wisely and graciously; and it is but <hi type="italic">for a season,</hi> and when need is, that we <hi type="italic">are in heaviness,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.6">1 Pet. i. 6</reference>. 4. That God has compassions and comforts in store even for those whom he has himself grieved. We must be far from thinking that, though God cause grief, the world will relieve and help us. No; the very same that caused the grief must bring in the favour, or we are undone. <hi type="italic">Una eademque manus vulnus opemque tulit—The same hand inflicted the wound and healed it.</hi> He has torn, and he will heal us, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">Hos. vi. 1</reference>. 5. That, when God returns to deal graciously with us, it will not be according to our merits, but according to his mercies, <hi type="italic">according to the multitude,</hi> the abundance, <hi type="italic">of his mercies.</hi> So unworthy we are that nothing but an abundant mercy will relieve us; and from that what may we not expect? And God's causing our grief ought to be no discouragement at all to those expectations. <div eID="gen18298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18299" type="x-p"/> VII. That, when God does cause grief, it is for wise and holy ends, and he takes not delight in our calamities, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.33">v. 33</reference>. He does indeed <hi type="italic">afflict, and grieve the children of men;</hi> all their grievances and afflictions are from him. But he does not do it <hi type="italic">willingly,</hi> not <hi type="italic">from the heart;</hi> so the word is. 1. He never afflicts us but when we give him cause to do it. He does not dispense his frowns as he does his favours, <hi type="italic">ex mero motu</hi>—<hi type="italic">from his mere good pleasure.</hi> If he show us kindness, it is because <hi type="italic">so it seems good</hi> unto him; but, if he write bitter things against us, it is because we both deserve them and need them. 2. He does not afflict with pleasure. He delights not in the death of sinners, or the disquiet of saints, but punishes with a kind of reluctance. He comes out of his place to punish, for his place is the mercy-seat. He delights not in the misery of any of his creatures, but, as it respects his own people, he is so far from it that in all their afflictions he is afflicted and his soul is grieved for the misery of Israel. 3. He retains his kindness for his people even when he afflicts them. If he does not <hi type="italic">willingly grieve the children of men,</hi> much less his own children. However it be, yet <hi type="italic">God is good</hi> to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Ps. lxxiii. 1</reference>), and they may by faith see love in his heart even when they see frowns in his face and a rod in his hand. <div eID="gen18299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18300" type="x-p"/> VIII. That though he makes use of men as his hand, or rather instruments in his hand, for the correcting of his people, yet he is far from being pleased with the injustice of their proceedings and the wrong they do them, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.34-Lam.3.36">v. 34-36</reference>. Though God serves his own purposes by the violence of wicked and unreasonable men, yet it does no therefore follow that he countenances that violence, as his oppressed people are sometimes tempted to think. <reference osisRef="Hab.1.3">Hab. i. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">Wherefore lookest thou upon those that deal treacherously?</hi> Two ways the people of God are injured and oppressed by their enemies, and the prophet here assures us that God does not approve of either of them:—1. If men injure them by force of arms, God does not approve of that. He does not himself <hi type="italic">crush under his feet the prisoners of the earth,</hi> but he regards the cry of the prisoners; nor does he approve of men's doing it; nay, he is much displeased with it. It is barbarous to trample on those that are down, and to crush those that are bound and cannot help themselves. 2. If men injure them under colour of law, and in the pretended administration of justice,—if they <hi type="italic">turn aside the right of a man,</hi> so that he cannot discover what his rights are or cannot come at them, they are out of his reach,—if they <hi type="italic">subvert a man in his cause,</hi> and bring in a wrong verdict, or give a false judgment, let them know, (1.) That God sees them. It is <hi type="italic">before the face of the Most High</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.35">v. 35</reference>); it is in his sight, under his eye, and is very displeasing to him. They cannot but know it is so, and therefore it is in defiance of him that they do it. He is <hi type="italic">the Most High,</hi> whose authority over them they contemn by abusing their authority over their subjects, not considering that <hi type="italic">he that is higher than the highest regardeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Eccl. v. 8</reference>. (2.) That God does not approve of them. More is implied than is expressed. The perverting of justice, and the subverting of the just, are a great affront to God; and, though he may make use of them for the correction of his people, yet he will sooner or later severely reckon with those that do thus. Note, However God may for a time suffer evil-doers to prosper, and serve his own purposes by them, yet he does not therefore approve of their evil doings. <hi type="italic">Far be it from God that he should do iniquity,</hi> or countenance those that do it.

<div eID="gen18300" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Duties of the Afflicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18301" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">37</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> he <hi type="italic">that</hi> saith, and it cometh to pass, <hi type="italic">when</hi> the Lord commandeth <hi type="italic">it</hi> not? <hi type="super">38</hi> Out of the mouth of the most High proceedeth not evil and good? <hi type="super">39</hi> Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins? <hi type="super">40</hi> Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">41</hi> Let us lift up our heart with <hi type="italic">our</hi> hands unto God in the heavens. <div eID="gen18301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18302" type="x-p"/> That we may be entitled to the comforts administered to the afflicted in the <reference osisRef="Lam.3.21-Lam.3.36">foregoing verses</reference>, and may taste the sweetness of them, we have here the duties of an afflicted state prescribed to us, in the performance of which we may expect those comforts. <div eID="gen18302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18303" type="x-p"/> I. We must see and acknowledge the hand of God in all the calamities that befal us at any time, whether personal or public, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.37-Lam.3.38">v. 37, 38</reference>. This is here laid down as a great truth, which will help to quiet our spirits under our afflictions and to sanctify them to us. 1. That, whatever men's actions are, it is God that overrules them: <hi type="italic">Who is he that saith, and it cometh to pass</hi> (that designs a thing and bring his designs to effect), if <hi type="italic">the Lord commandeth it not?</hi> Men can do nothing but according to the counsel of God, nor have any power or success but what is given them from above. <hi type="italic">A man's heart devises his way;</hi> he projects and purposes; he says that he will do so and so (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.13">Jam. iv. 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">but the Lord directs his steps</hi> far otherwise than he designed them, and what he contrived and expected does not <hi type="italic">come to pass,</hi> unless it be what God's hand and his counsel had determined before to be done, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.9">Prov. xvi. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.23">Jer. x. 23</reference>. The Chaldeans said that they would destroy Jerusalem, and it came to pass, not because they said it, but because God commanded it and commissioned them to do it. Note, Men are but tools which the great God makes use of, and manages as he pleases, in the government of this lower world; and they cannot accomplish any of their designs without him. 2. That, whatever men's lot is, it is God that orders it: <hi type="italic">Out of the mouth of the Most High do not evil and good proceed?</hi> Yes, certainly they do; and it is more emphatically expressed in the original: <hi type="italic">Do not</hi> this <hi type="italic">evil, and</hi> this <hi type="italic">good, proceed out of the mouth of the Most High?</hi> Is it not what he has ordained and appointed for us? Yes, certainly it is; and for the reconciling of us to our own afflictions, whatever they be, this general truth must thus be particularly applied. This comfort I receive <hi type="italic">from the hand of God, and shall I not receive</hi> that <hi type="italic">evil</hi> also? so Job argues, <reference osisRef="Job.2.10">ch. ii. 10</reference>. Are we healthful or sickly, rich or poor? Do we succeed in our designs, or are we crossed in them? It is all what God orders; <hi type="italic">every man's judgment proceeds from him. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away;</hi> he forms the light and creates the darkness, as he did at first. Note, All the events of divine Providence are the products of a divine counsel; whatever is done God has the directing of it, and the works of his hands agree with the words of his mouth; <hi type="italic">he speaks, and it is done,</hi> so easily, so effectually are all his purposes fulfilled. <div eID="gen18303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18304" type="x-p"/> II. We must not quarrel with God for any affliction that he lays upon us at any time (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore does a living man complain?</hi> The prophet here seems to check himself for the complaint he had made in the former part of the chapter, wherein he seemed to reflect upon God as unkind and severe. "Do I well to be angry? Why do I fret thus?" Those who in their haste have chidden with God must, in the reflection, chide themselves for it. From the doctrine of God's sovereign and universal providence, which he had asserted in the <reference osisRef="Lam.3.21-Lam.3.36">verses before</reference>, he draws this inference, <hi type="italic">Wherefore does a living man complain?</hi> What God does we must not open our mouths against, <reference osisRef="Ps.39.9">Ps. xxxix. 9</reference>. Those that blame their lot reproach him that allotted it to them. The sufferers in the captivity must submit to the will of God in all their sufferings. Note, Though we may pour out our complaints before God, we must never exhibit any complaints against God. What! Shall <hi type="italic">a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?</hi> The reasons here urged are very cogent. 1. We are men; let us herein show ourselves men. Shall <hi type="italic">a man complain?</hi> And again, <hi type="italic">a man!</hi> We are men, and not brutes, reasonable creatures, who should act with reason, who should look upward and look forward, and both ways may fetch considerations enough to silence our complaints. We are men, and not children that cry for every thing that hurts them. We are men, and not gods, subjects, not lords; we are not our own masters, not our own carvers; we are bound and must obey, must submit. We are men, and not angels, and therefore cannot expect to be free from troubles as they are; we are not inhabitants of that world where there is no sorrow, but this where there is nothing but sorrow. We are men, and not devils, are not in that deplorable, helpless, hopeless, state that they are in, but have something to comfort ourselves with which they have not. 2. We are living men. Through the good hand of our God upon us we are alive yet, though dying daily; and shall <hi type="italic">a living man complain?</hi> No; he has more reason to be thankful for life than to complain of any of the burdens and calamities of life. Our lives are frail and forfeited, and yet we are alive; now <hi type="italic">the living, the living, they</hi> should <hi type="italic">praise,</hi> and not complain (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.19">Isa. xxxviii. 19</reference>); while there is life there is hope, and therefore, instead of complaining that things are bad, we should encourage ourselves with the hope that they will be better. 3. We are sinful men, and that which we complain of is the just <hi type="italic">punishment of our sins;</hi> nay, it is far less than our iniquities have deserved. We have little reason to complain of our trouble, for it is our own doing; we may thank ourselves. Our own wickedness corrects us, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.3">Prov. xix. 3</reference>. We have no reason to quarrel with God, for he is righteous in it; he is the governor of the world, and it is necessary that he should maintain the honour of his government by chastising the disobedient. Are we suffering for our sins? Then let us not complain; for we have other work to do; instead of repining, we must be repenting; and, as an evidence that God is reconciled to us, we must be endeavouring to reconcile ourselves to his holy will. Are we <hi type="italic">punished for our sins?</hi> It is our wisdom then to submit, and to kiss the rod; for, if we still walk contrary to God, he will punish us yet seven times more; for <hi type="italic">when he judges he will overcome.</hi> But, if we accommodate ourselves to him, though we be <hi type="italic">chastened of the Lord</hi> we shall not be <hi type="italic">condemned with the world.</hi> <div eID="gen18304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18305" type="x-p"/> III. We must set ourselves to answer God's intention in afflicting us, which is to bring sin to our remembrance, and to bring us home to himself, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.40">v. 40</reference>. These are the two things which our afflictions should put us upon. 1. A serious consideration of ourselves and a reflection upon our past lives. <hi type="italic">Let us search and try our ways,</hi> search what they have been, and then try whether they have been right and good or no; search as for a malefactor in disguise, that flees and hides himself, and then try whether guilty or not guilty. Let conscience be employed both to search and to try, and let it have leave to deal faithfully, to accomplish a diligent search and to make an impartial trial. <hi type="italic">Let us try our ways,</hi> that by them we may try ourselves, for we are to judge of our state not by our faint wishes, but by our steps, not by one particular step, but by our ways, the ends we aim at, the rules we go by, and the agreeableness of the temper of our minds and the tenour of our lives to those ends and those rules. When we are in affliction it is seasonable to <hi type="italic">consider our ways</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.5">Hag. i. 5</reference>), that what is amiss may be repented of and amended for the future, and so we may answer the intention of the affliction. We are apt, in times of public calamity, to reflect upon other people's ways, and lay blame upon them; whereas our business is to <hi type="italic">search and try our</hi> own <hi type="italic">ways.</hi> We have work enough to do at home; we must each of us say, "What have I done? What have I contributed to the public flames?" that we may each of us mend one, and then we should all be mended. 2. A sincere conversion to God: "Let us <hi type="italic">turn again to the Lord,</hi> to him who is turned against us and whom we have turned from; to him let us turn by repentance and reformation, as to our owner and ruler. We have been with him, and it has never been well with us since we forsook him; let us therefore now turn again to him." This must accompany the former and be the fruit of it; <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> we must <hi type="italic">search and try our ways,</hi> that we may turn from the evil of them to God. This was the method David took. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.59">Ps. cxix. 59</reference>, <hi type="italic">I thought on my ways, and turned my feet unto thy testimonies.</hi> <div eID="gen18305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18306" type="x-p"/> IV. We must offer up ourselves to God, and our best affections and services, in the flames of devotion, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.41">v. 41</reference>. When we are in affliction, 1. We must look up to God as a <hi type="italic">God in the heavens,</hi> infinitely above us, and who has an incontestable dominion over us; for <hi type="italic">the heavens do rule,</hi> and are therefore not to be quarrelled with, but submitted to. 2. We must pray to him, with a believing expectation to receive mercy from him; for that is implied in our <hi type="italic">lifting up our hands</hi> to him (a gesture commonly used in prayer and sometimes put for it, as <reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Ps. cxli. 2</reference>, <hi type="italic">Let the lifting up of my hands be as the evening sacrifice</hi>); it signifies our requesting mercy from him and our readiness to receive that mercy. (3.) Our hearts must go along with our prayers. We must <hi type="italic">lift up our hearts with our hands,</hi> as we must pour out our souls with our words. It is the heart that God looks at in that and every other service; for what will a sacrifice without a heart avail? If inward impressions be not in some measure answerable to outward expressions, we do but mock God and deceive ourselves. Praying is lifting up the soul to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Ps. xxv. 1</reference>) as to <hi type="italic">our Father in heaven;</hi> and the soul that hopes to be with God in heaven for ever will thus, by frequent acts of devotion, be still learning the way thither and pressing forward in that way.

<div eID="gen18306" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaining to God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18307" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">42</hi> We have transgressed and have rebelled: thou hast not pardoned. <hi type="super">43</hi> Thou hast covered with anger, and persecuted us: thou hast slain, thou hast not pitied. <hi type="super">44</hi> Thou hast covered thyself with a cloud, that <hi type="italic">our</hi> prayer should not pass through. <hi type="super">45</hi> Thou hast made us <hi type="italic">as</hi> the offscouring and refuse in the midst of the people. <hi type="super">46</hi> All our enemies have opened their mouths against us. <hi type="super">47</hi> Fear and a snare is come upon us, desolation and destruction. <hi type="super">48</hi> Mine eye runneth down with rivers of water for the destruction of the daughter of my people. <hi type="super">49</hi> Mine eye trickleth down, and ceaseth not, without any intermission, <hi type="super">50</hi> Till the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> look down, and behold from heaven. <hi type="super">51</hi> Mine eye affecteth mine heart because of all the daughters of my city. <hi type="super">52</hi> Mine enemies chased me sore, like a bird, without cause. <hi type="super">53</hi> They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me. <hi type="super">54</hi> Waters flowed over mine head; <hi type="italic">then</hi> I said, I am cut off. <div eID="gen18307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18308" type="x-p"/> It is easier to chide ourselves for complaining than to chide ourselves out of it. The prophet had owned that a living man should not complain, as if he checked himself for his complaints in the former part of the chapter; and yet here the clouds return after the rain and the wound bleeds afresh; for great pains must be taken with a troubled spirit to bring it into temper. <div eID="gen18308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18309" type="x-p"/> I. They confess the righteousness of God in afflicting them (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.42">v. 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">We have transgressed and have rebelled.</hi> Note, It becomes us, when we are in trouble, to justify God, by owning our sins, and laying the load upon ourselves for them. Call sin a transgression, call it a rebellion, and you do not miscall it. This is the result of their searching and trying their ways; the more they enquired into them the worse they found them. Yet, <div eID="gen18309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18310" type="x-p"/> II. They complain of the afflictions they are under, not without some reflections upon God, which we are not to imitate, but, under the sharpest trials, must always think and speak highly and kindly of him. <div eID="gen18310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18311" type="x-p"/> 1. They complain of his frowns and the tokens of his displeasure against them. Their sins were repented of, and yet (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.42">v. 42</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou hast not pardoned.</hi> They had not the assurance and comfort of the pardon; the judgments brought upon them for their sins were not removed, and therefore they thought they could not say the sin was pardoned, which was a mistake, but a common mistake with the people of God when their souls are cast down and disquieted within them. Their case was really pitiable, yet they complain, <hi type="italic">Thou hast not pitied,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.43">v. 43</reference>. Their enemies persecuted and slew them, but that was not the worst of it; they were but the instruments in God's hand: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast persecuted us, and thou hast slain us,</hi> though we expected thou wouldst protect and deliver us." They complain that there was a wall of partition between them and God, and, (1.) This hindered God's favours from coming down upon them. The reflected beams of God's kindness to them used to be the beauty of Israel; but now "<hi type="italic">thou hast covered</hi> us <hi type="italic">with anger,</hi> so that our glory is concealed and gone; now God is angry with us, and we do not appear that illustrious people that we have formerly been thought to be." Or, "<hi type="italic">Thou hast covered us</hi> up as men that are buried are covered up and forgotten." (2.) It hindered their prayers from coming up unto God (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.44">v. 44</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast covered thyself with a cloud,</hi>" not like that bright cloud in which he took possession of the temple, which enabled the worshippers to draw near to him, but like that in which he came down upon Mount Sinai, which obliged the people to stand at a distance. "This cloud is so thick <hi type="italic">that our prayers</hi> seem as if they were lost in it; they cannot <hi type="italic">pass through;</hi> we cannot obtain an audience." Note, The prolonging of troubles is sometimes a temptation, even to praying people, to question whether God be what they have always believed him to be, a prayer-hearing God. <div eID="gen18311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18312" type="x-p"/> 2. They complain of the contempt of their neighbours and the reproach and ignominy they were under (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.45">v. 45</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou hast made us as the off-scouring,</hi> or scrapings, of the first floor, which are thrown to the dunghill." This St. Paul refers to in his account of the sufferings of the apostles. <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.13">1 Cor. iv. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">We are made as the filth of the world and are the off-scouring of all things.</hi> "We are the <hi type="italic">refuse,</hi> or dross, <hi type="italic">in the midst of the people,</hi> trodden upon by every body, and looked upon as the vilest of the nations, and good for nothing but to be cast out as <hi type="italic">salt</hi> which <hi type="italic">has lost its savour. Our enemies have opened their mouths against us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.46">v. 46</reference>), have <hi type="italic">gaped upon us as roaring lions,</hi> to swallow us up, or made mouths at us, or have taken liberty to say what they please of us." These complaints we had before, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15-Lam.2.16">ch. ii. 15, 16</reference>. Note, It is common for base and ill-natured men to run upon, and run down, those that have fallen into the depths of distress from the height of honour. But this they brought upon themselves by sin. If they had not made themselves vile, their enemies could not have made them so: but <hi type="italic">therefore men call them reprobate silver, because the Lord has rejected them</hi> for rejecting him. <div eID="gen18312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18313" type="x-p"/> 3. They complain of the lamentable destruction that their enemies made of them (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.47">v. 47</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fear and a snare have come upon us;</hi> the enemies have not only terrified us with those alarms, but prevailed against us by their stratagems, and surprised us with the ambushes they laid for us; and then follows nothing but <hi type="italic">desolation and destruction,</hi> the <hi type="italic">destruction of the daughter of my people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.48">v. 48</reference>), <hi type="italic">of all the daughters of my city,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.51">v. 51</reference>. The enemies, having taken some of them <hi type="italic">like a bird</hi> in a snare, <hi type="italic">chased</hi> others as a harmless bird is chased by a bird of prey (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.52">v. 52</reference>): <hi type="italic">My enemies chased me sorely like a bird</hi> which is beaten from bush to bush, as Saul hunted David <hi type="italic">like a partridge.</hi> Thus restless was the enmity of their persecutors, and yet causeless. They have done it <hi type="italic">without cause,</hi> without any provocation given them. Though God was righteous, they were unrighteous. David often complains of those that <hi type="italic">hated him without cause;</hi> and such are the enemies of Christ and his church, <reference osisRef="John.15.25">John xv. 25</reference>. Their enemies chased them till they had quite prevailed over them (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.53">v. 53</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have cut off my life in the dungeon.</hi> They have shut up their captives in close and dark prisons, where they are as it were cut off <hi type="italic">from the land of the living</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Lam.3.6">v. 6</reference>), or the state and kingdom are sunk and ruined, the life and being of them are gone, and they are as it were thrown into the dungeon or grave and a <hi type="italic">stone cast upon them,</hi> such as used to be <hi type="italic">rolled to the door of the sepulchres.</hi> They look upon the Jewish nation as dead and buried, and imagine that there is not possibility of its resurrection. Thus Ezekiel saw it, in vision, <hi type="italic">a valley full of dead and dry bones.</hi> Their destruction is compared not only to the burying of a dead man, but to the sinking of a living man into the water, who cannot long be a living man there, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.54">v. 54</reference>. <hi type="italic">Waters</hi> of affliction <hi type="italic">flowed over my head.</hi> The deluge prevailed and quite overwhelmed them. The Chaldean forces broke in upon them <hi type="italic">as the breaking forth of waters,</hi> which rose so high as to <hi type="italic">flow over their heads;</hi> they could not wade, they could not swim, and therefore must unavoidably sink. Note, The distresses of God's people sometimes prevail to such a degree that they cannot find any footing for their faith, nor keep their head above water, with any comfortable expectation. <div eID="gen18313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18314" type="x-p"/> 4. They complain of their own excessive grief and fear upon this account. (1.) The afflicted church is drowned in tears, and the prophet for her (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.48-Lam.3.49">v. 48, 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">My eye runs down with rivers of water,</hi> so abundant was their weeping; <hi type="italic">it trickles down and ceases not,</hi> so constant was their weeping, <hi type="italic">without</hi> any <hi type="italic">intermission,</hi> there being no relaxation of their miseries. The distemper was in continual extremity, and they had no better day. It is added (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.51">v. 51</reference>), "<hi type="italic">My eye affects my heart.</hi> My seeing eye affects my heart. The more I look upon the desolation of the city and country the more I am grieved. Which way soever I cast my eye, I see that which renews my sorrow, even <hi type="italic">because of all the daughters of my city,</hi>" all the neighbouring towns, which were as daughters to Jerusalem the mother-city.
