Or, <hi type="italic">My weeping eye affects my heart;</hi> the venting of the grief, instead of easing it, did but increase and exasperate it. Or, <hi type="italic">My eye melts my soul;</hi> I have quite wept away my spirits; not only <hi type="italic">my eye is consumed with grief, but my soul and my life are spent with it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.31.9-Ps.31.10">Ps. xxxi. 9, 10</reference>. Great and long grief exhausts the spirits, and brings not only many a <hi type="italic">gray head,</hi> but many a green head too, <hi type="italic">to the grave.</hi> I weep, ways the prophet, <hi type="italic">more than all the daughters of my city</hi> (so the margin reads it); he outdid even those of the tender sex in the expressions of grief. And it is no diminution to any to be much in tears for the sins of sinners and the sufferings of saints; our Lord Jesus was so; for, <hi type="italic">when he came near, he beheld</hi> this same <hi type="italic">city and wept over it,</hi> which the daughters of Jerusalem did not. (2.) She is overwhelmed with fears, not only grieves for what is, but fears worse, and gives up all for gone (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.54">v. 54</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Then I said, I am cut off,</hi> ruined, and see no hope of recovery; I am as one dead." Note, Those that are cast down are commonly tempted to think themselves cast off, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.22">Ps. xxxi. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">Jon. ii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen18314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18315" type="x-p"/> 5. In the midst of these sad complaints here is one word of comfort, by which it appears that their case was not altogether so bad as they made it, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.50">v. 50</reference>. We continue thus weeping <hi type="italic">till the Lord look down and behold from heaven.</hi> This intimates, (1.) That they were satisfied that God's gracious regard to them in their miseries would be an effectual redress of all their grievances. "If God, who now <hi type="italic">covers himself with a cloud,</hi> as if he took no notice of our troubles (<reference osisRef="Job.22.13">Job xxii. 13</reference>), would but shine forth, all would be well; if he look upon us, <hi type="italic">we shall be saved,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.80.19">Ps. lxxx. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.17">Dan. ix. 17</reference>. Bad as the case is, one favourable look from heaven will set all to rights. (2.) That they had hopes that he would at length look graciously upon them and relieve them; nay, they take it for granted that he will: "Though he contend long, he will not contend for ever, thou we deserve that he should." (3.) That while they continued weeping they continued waiting, and neither did nor would expect relief and succour from any hand but his; nothing shall comfort them but his gracious returns, nor shall any thing wipe tears from their eyes <hi type="italic">till he look down.</hi> Their eyes, which now <hi type="italic">run down with water,</hi> shall still <hi type="italic">wait upon the Lord their God until he have mercy upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.123.2">Ps. cxxiii. 2</reference>.

<div eID="gen18315" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Goodness Acknowledged; An Appeal to God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18316" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">55</hi> I called upon thy name, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , out of the low dungeon. <hi type="super">56</hi> Thou hast heard my voice: hide not thine ear at my breathing, at my cry. <hi type="super">57</hi> Thou drewest near in the day <hi type="italic">that</hi> I called upon thee: thou saidst, Fear not. <hi type="super">58</hi> O Lord, thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul; thou hast redeemed my life. <hi type="super">59</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , thou hast seen my wrong: judge thou my cause. <hi type="super">60</hi> Thou hast seen all their vengeance <hi type="italic">and</hi> all their imaginations against me. <hi type="super">61</hi> Thou hast heard their reproach, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">and</hi> all their imaginations against me; <hi type="super">62</hi> The lips of those that rose up against me, and their device against me all the day. <hi type="super">63</hi> Behold their sitting down, and their rising up; I <hi type="italic">am</hi> their music. <hi type="super">64</hi> Render unto them a recompence, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , according to the work of their hands. <hi type="super">65</hi> Give them sorrow of heart, thy curse unto them. <hi type="super">66</hi> Persecute and destroy them in anger from under the heavens of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen18316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18317" type="x-p"/> We may observe throughout this chapter a struggle in the prophet's breast between sense and faith, fear and hope; he complains and then comforts himself, yet drops his comforts and returns again to his complaints, as <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1-Ps.42.11">Ps. xlii</reference>. But, as there, so here, faith gets the last word and comes off a conqueror; for in these verses he concludes with some comfort. And here are two things with which he comforts himself:— <div eID="gen18317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18318" type="x-p"/> I. His experience of God's goodness even in his affliction. This may refer to the prophet's personal experience, with which he encourages himself in reference to the public troubles. He that has seasonably succoured particular saints will not fail the church in general. Or it may include the remnant of good people that were among the Jews, who had found that it was not in vain to wait upon God. In three things the prophet and his pious friends had found God good to them:—1. He had <hi type="italic">heard their prayers;</hi> though they had been ready to fear that the cloud of wrath was such as their <hi type="italic">prayers could not pass through</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.44">v. 44</reference>), yet upon second thoughts, or at least upon further trial, they find it otherwise, and that God had not said unto them, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain.</hi> When they were <hi type="italic">in the low dungeon,</hi> as <hi type="italic">free among the dead,</hi> they <hi type="italic">called upon God's name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.55">v. 55</reference>); their weeping did not hinder praying. Note, Though we are cast into ever so low a dungeon, we may thence find a way of access to God in the highest heavens. <hi type="italic">Out of the depths have I cried unto thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.1">Ps. cxxx. 1</reference>), as Jonah out of the whale's belly. And could God hear them out of the low dungeon, and would he? Yes, he did: <hi type="italic">Thou hast heard my voice;</hi> and some read the following words as carrying on the same thankful acknowledgment: <hi type="italic">Thou didst not hide thy ear at my breathing, at my cry;</hi> and the original will bear that reading. We read it as a petition for further audience: <hi type="italic">Hide not thy ear.</hi> God's having heard our voice when we <hi type="italic">cried to him,</hi> even out of <hi type="italic">the low dungeon,</hi> is an encouragement for us to hope that he will not at any time <hi type="italic">hide his ear.</hi> Observe how he calls prayer <hi type="italic">his breathing;</hi> for in prayer we breathe towards God, we breathe after him. Though we be but weak in prayer, cannot cry aloud, but only <hi type="italic">breathe</hi> in <hi type="italic">groanings that cannot be uttered,</hi> yet we shall not be neglected if we be sincere. Prayer is the breath of the new man, sucking in the air of mercy in petitions and returning it in praises; it is both the evidence and the maintenance of the spiritual life. Some read it, <hi type="italic">at my gasping.</hi> "When I lay gasping for life, and ready to expire, and thought i was breathing my last, then thou tookest cognizance of my distressed case." 2. He had silenced their fears and quieted their spirits (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.57">v. 57</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou drewest near in the day that I called upon thee;</hi> thou didst graciously assure me of thy presence with me, and give me to see thee nigh unto me, whereas I had thought thee to be at a distance from me." Note, When we draw nigh to God in a way of duty we may by faith see him drawing nigh to us in a way of mercy. But this was not all: <hi type="italic">Thou saidst, Fear not.</hi> This was the language of God's prophets preaching to them not to fear (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.10">Isa. xli. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.14">14</reference>), of his providence preventing those things which they were afraid of, and of his grace quieting their minds, and making them easy, by the witness of his Spirit with their spirits that they were his people still, though in distress, and therefore ought not to fear. 3. He had already begun to appear for them (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.58">v. 58</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O Lord! thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul</hi>" (that is, as it follows), "<hi type="italic">thou hast redeemed my life,</hi> hast rescued that out of the hands of those who would have taken it away, hast saved that when it was ready to be swallowed up, hast given me that for a prey." And this is an encouragement to them to hope that he would yet further appear for them: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast delivered my soul from death,</hi> and therefore wilt deliver <hi type="italic">my feet from falling;</hi> thou hast <hi type="italic">pleaded the causes of my life,</hi> and therefore wilt plead my other causes." <div eID="gen18318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18319" type="x-p"/> II. He comforts himself with an appeal to God's justice, and (in order to the sentence of that) to his omniscience. <div eID="gen18319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18320" type="x-p"/> 1. He appeals to God's knowledge of the matter of fact, how very spiteful and malicious his enemies were (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.59">v. 59</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O Lord! thou hast seen my wrong,</hi> that I have done no wrong at all, but suffer a great deal." He that knows all things knew, (1.) The malice they had against him: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast seen all their vengeance,</hi> how they desire to do me a mischief, as if it were by way of reprisal for some great injury I had done them." Note, We should consider, to our terror and caution, that God knows all the revengeful thoughts we have in our minds against others, and therefore we should not allow of those thoughts nor harbour them, and that he knows all the revengeful thoughts others have causelessly in their minds against us, and therefore we should not be afraid of them, but leave it to him to protect us from them. (2.) The designs and projects they had laid to do him a mischief: <hi type="italic">Thou hast seen all their imaginations against me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.60">v. 60</reference>), and again, "<hi type="italic">Thou hast heard all their imaginations against me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.61">v. 61</reference>), both the desire and the device they have to ruin me; whether it show itself in word or deed, it is known to thee; nay, though the products of it are not to be seen nor heard, yet their device against me all the day is perceived and understood by him to whom all things are naked and open." Note, The most secret contrivances of the church's enemies are perfectly known to the church's God, from whom they can hide nothing. (3.) The contempt and calumny wherewith they loaded him, all that they spoke slightly of him, and all that they spoke reproachfully: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast heard their reproach</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.61">v. 61</reference>), all the bad characters they give me, laying to my charge things that I know not, all the methods they use to make me odious and contemptible, even the <hi type="italic">lips of those that rose up against me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.62">v. 62</reference>), the contumelious language they use whenever they speak of me, and that at their sitting down and rising up, when they lie down at night and get up in the morning, when they sit down to their meat and with their company, and when they rise from both, still I am their music; they make themselves and one another merry with my miseries, as the Philistines made sport with Samson." Jerusalem was the tabret they played upon. Perhaps they had some tune or play, some opera or interlude, that was called <hi type="italic">the destruction of Jerusalem,</hi> which, though in the nature of a tragedy, was very entertaining to those who wished ill to the holy city. Note, God will one day call sinners to account for all the hard speeches which they have spoken against him and his people, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. <div eID="gen18320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18321" type="x-p"/> 2. He appeals to God's judgment upon this fact: "<hi type="italic">Lord, thou hast seen my wrong;</hi> there is no need of any evidence to prove it, nor any prosecutor to enforce and aggravate it; thou seest it in its true colours; and now I leave it with thee. <hi type="italic">Judge thou my cause,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.59">v. 59</reference>. Let them be dealt with," (1.) "As they deserve (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.64">v. 64</reference>): <hi type="italic">Render to them a recompence according to the work of their hands.</hi> Let them be dealt with as they have dealt with us; let thy hand be against them as their hand has been against us. They have created us a great deal of vexation; now, Lord, <hi type="italic">give them sorrow of heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.65">v. 65</reference>), <hi type="italic">perplexity of heart</hi>" (so some read it); "let them be surrounded with threatening mischiefs on all sides, and not be able to see their way out. Give them <hi type="italic">despondence of heart</hi>" (so others read it); "let them be driven to despair, and give themselves up for gone." God can entangle the head that thinks itself clearest, and sink the heart that thinks itself stoutest. (2.) "Let them be dealt with according to the threatenings: <hi type="italic">Thy curse unto them;</hi> that is, let thy curse come upon them, all the evils that are pronounced in thy word against the enemies of thy people, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.65">v. 65</reference>. They have loaded us with curses; as they loved cursing, so let it come unto them, thy curse which will make them truly miserable. Theirs is causeless, and therefore fruitless, it shall not come; but thine is just, and shall take effect. Those whom thou cursest are cursed indeed. Let the curse be executed, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.66">v. 66</reference>. <hi type="italic">Persecute and destroy them in anger,</hi> as they persecute and destroy us in their anger. <hi type="italic">Destroy them from under the heavens of the Lord;</hi> let them have no benefit of the light and influence of the heavens. Destroy them in such a manner that all who see it may say, It is a destruction from the Almighty, who <hi type="italic">sits in the heavens and laughs at them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Ps. ii. 4</reference>), and may own <hi type="italic">that the heavens do rule,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Dan.4.26">Dan. iv. 26</reference>. What is said of the idols is here said of their worshippers (who in this also shall be like unto them), <hi type="italic">They shall perish from under these heavens,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.10.11">Jer. x. 11</reference>. They shall be not only excluded from the happiness of the invisible heavens, but cut off from the comfort even of these visible ones, which are the <hi type="italic">heavens of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.16">Ps. cxv. 16</reference>) and which those therefore are unworthy to be taken under the protection of who rebel against him.  <chapter eID="Lam.3"/> <div eID="gen18321" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen18324" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18323" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Desolate Condition of Jerusalem; Effects of Famine in Jerusalem; Destruction of Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  588.)</title> <div sID="gen18325" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> How is the gold become dim! <hi type="italic">how</hi> is the most fine gold changed! the stones of the sanctuary are poured out in the top of every street. <hi type="super">2</hi> The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter! <hi type="super">3</hi> Even the sea monsters draw out the breast, they give suck to their young ones: the daughter of my people <hi type="italic">is become</hi> cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness. <hi type="super">4</hi> The tongue of the sucking child cleaveth to the roof of his mouth for thirst: the young children ask bread, <hi type="italic">and</hi> no man breaketh <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto them. <hi type="super">5</hi> They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills. <hi type="super">6</hi> For the punishment of the iniquity of the daughter of my people is greater than the punishment of the sin of Sodom, that was overthrown as in a moment, and no hands stayed on her. <hi type="super">7</hi> Her Nazarites were purer than snow, they were whiter than milk, they were more ruddy in body than rubies, their polishing <hi type="italic">was</hi> of sapphire: <hi type="super">8</hi> Their visage is blacker than a coal; they are not known in the streets: their skin cleaveth to their bones; it is withered, it is become like a stick. <hi type="super">9</hi> <hi type="italic">They that be</hi> slain with the sword are better than <hi type="italic">they that be</hi> slain with hunger: for these pine away, stricken through for <hi type="italic">want of</hi> the fruits of the field. <hi type="super">10</hi> The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children: they were their meat in the destruction of the daughter of my people. <hi type="super">11</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath accomplished his fury; he hath poured out his fierce anger, and hath kindled a fire in Zion, and it hath devoured the foundations thereof. <hi type="super">12</hi> The kings of the earth, and all the inhabitants of the world, would not have believed that the adversary and the enemy should have entered into the gates of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen18325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18326" type="x-p"/> The elegy in this chapter begins with a lamentation of the very sad and doleful change which the judgments of God had made in Jerusalem. The city that was formerly <hi type="italic">as gold,</hi> as <hi type="italic">the most fine gold,</hi> so rich and splendid, <hi type="italic">the perfection of beauty and the joy of the whole earth,</hi> has become dim, and is changed, has lost its lustre, lost its value, is not what it was; it has become dross. Alas! what an alteration is here! <div eID="gen18326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18327" type="x-p"/> I. The temple was laid waste, which was the glory of Jerusalem and its protection. It is given up into the hands of the enemy. And some understand the gold spoken of (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.1">v. 1</reference>) to be the <hi type="italic">gold of the temple,</hi> the fine gold with which it was overlaid (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.22">1 Kings vi. 22</reference>); when the temple was burned the gold of it was smoked and sullied, as if it had been of little value. It was thrown among the rubbish; it <hi type="italic">was changed,</hi> converted to common uses and made nothing of. <hi type="italic">The stones of the sanctuary,</hi> which were curiously wrought, were thrown down by the Chaldeans, when they demolished it, or were brought down by the force of the fire, and were <hi type="italic">poured out,</hi> and thrown about <hi type="italic">in the top of every street;</hi> they lay mingled without distinction among the common ruins. When the God of the sanctuary was by sin provoked to withdraw no wonder that the stones of the sanctuary were thus profaned. <div eID="gen18327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18328" type="x-p"/> II. The princes and priests, who were in a special manner the <hi type="italic">sons of Zion,</hi> were trampled upon and abused, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.2">v. 2</reference>. Both the house of God and the house of David were in Zion. The sons of both those houses were upon this account precious, that they were heirs to the privileges of those two covenants of priesthood and royalty. They were <hi type="italic">comparable to fine gold.</hi> Israel was more rich in them than in treasures of gold and silver. But now they are <hi type="italic">esteemed as earthen pitchers;</hi> they are broken as <hi type="italic">earthen pitchers,</hi> thrown by as vessels in which there is no pleasure. They have grown poor, and are brought into captivity, and thereby are rendered mean and despicable, and every one treads upon them and insults over them. Note, The contempt put upon God's people ought to be matter of lamentation to us. <div eID="gen18328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18329" type="x-p"/> III. Little children were starved for want of bread and water, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.3-Lam.4.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. The nursing-mothers, having no meat for themselves, had no milk for the babes at their breast, so that, though in disposition they were really compassionate, yet in fact they seemed to be cruel, <hi type="italic">like the ostriches in the wilderness, that leave their eggs in the dust</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.39.14-Job.39.15">Job xxxix. 14, 15</reference>); having no food for their children, they were forced to neglect them and do what they could to forget them, because it was a pain to them to think of them when they had nothing for them; in this they were worse than the seals, or <hi type="italic">sea-monsters,</hi> or <hi type="italic">whales</hi> (as some render it), for they <hi type="italic">drew out the breast, and gave suck to their young,</hi> which <hi type="italic">the daughter of my people</hi> will not do. Children cannot shift for themselves as grown people can; and therefore it was the more painful to see <hi type="italic">the tongue of the sucking-child cleave to the roof of his mouth for thirst,</hi> because there was not a drop of water to moisten it; and to hear the young children, that could but just speak, <hi type="italic">ask bread</hi> of their parents, who had none to give them, no, nor any friend that could supply them. As doleful as our thoughts are of this case, so thankful should our thoughts be of the great plenty we enjoy, and the food convenient we have for ourselves and for our children, and for <hi type="italic">those of our own house.</hi> <div eID="gen18329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18330" type="x-p"/> IV. Persons of good rank were reduced to extreme poverty, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.5">v. 5</reference>. Those who were well-born and well bred, and had been accustomed to the best, both for food and clothing, who had <hi type="italic">fed delicately,</hi> had every thing that was curious and nice (they call it <hi type="italic">eating well,</hi> whereas those only eat well who eat to the glory of God), and <hi type="italic">fared sumptuously every day;</hi> they had not only been <hi type="italic">advanced to the scarlet,</hi> but from their beginning were <hi type="italic">brought up in scarlet,</hi> and were never acquainted with any thing mean or ordinary. They were <hi type="italic">brought up upon scarlet</hi> (so the word is); their foot-cloths, and the carpets they walked on, were scarlet, yet these, being stripped of all by the war, are <hi type="italic">desolate in the streets,</hi> have not a house to put their head in, nor a bed to lie on, nor clothes to cover them, nor fire to warm them. They <hi type="italic">embrace dunghills;</hi> on them they were glad to lie to get a little rest, and perhaps raked in the dunghills for something to eat, as the prodigal son who <hi type="italic">would fain have filled his belly with the husks.</hi> Note, Those who live in the greatest pomp and plenty know not what straits they may be reduced to before they die; as sometimes the <hi type="italic">needy</hi> are <hi type="italic">raised out of the dunghill. Those who were full have hired out themselves for bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.5">1 Sam. ii. 5</reference>. It is therefore the wisdom of those who have abundance not to use themselves too nicely, for then hardships, when they come, will be doubly hard, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.56">Deut. xxviii. 56</reference>. <div eID="gen18330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18331" type="x-p"/> V. Persons who were eminent for dignity, nay, perhaps for sanctity, shared with others in the common calamity, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.7-Lam.4.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Her Nazarites</hi> are extremely charged. Some understand it only of her honourable ones, the young gentlemen, who were very clean, and neat, and well-dressed, washed and perfumed; but I see not why we may not understand it of those devout people among them who <hi type="italic">separated themselves to the Lord</hi> by the <hi type="italic">Nazarites'</hi> vow, <reference osisRef="Num.6.2">Num. vi. 2</reference>. That there were such among them in the most degenerate times appears from <reference osisRef="Amos.2.11">Amos ii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">I raised up of your young men for Nazarites.</hi> These <hi type="italic">Nazarites,</hi> though they were not to cut their hair, yet by reason of their temperate diet, their frequent washings, and especially the pleasure they had in devoting themselves to God and conversing with him, which made their faces to shine as <hi type="italic">Moses's,</hi> were <hi type="italic">purer than snow</hi> and <hi type="italic">whiter than milk;</hi> drinking no wine nor strong drink, they had a more healthful complexion and cheerful countenance than those who regaled themselves daily with the blood of the grape, as <hi type="italic">Daniel</hi> and his fellows with <hi type="italic">pulse and water.</hi> Or it may denote the great respect and veneration which all good people had for them; though perhaps to the eye they had <hi type="italic">no form nor comeliness,</hi> yet, being separated to the Lord, they were valued as if they had been <hi type="italic">more ruddy than rubies and their polishing had been of sapphire.</hi> But now <hi type="italic">their visage is marred</hi> (as is said of Christ, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.14">Isa. lii. 14</reference>); it is <hi type="italic">blacker than a coal;</hi> they look miserably, partly through hunger and partly through grief and perplexity. <hi type="italic">They are not known in the streets;</hi> those who respected them now take no notice of them, and those who had been intimately acquainted with them now scarcely knew them, their countenance was so altered by the miseries that attended the long siege. <hi type="italic">Their skin cleaves to their bones,</hi> their flesh being quite consumed and wasted away; it is <hi type="italic">withered;</hi> it has <hi type="italic">become like a stick,</hi> as dry and hard as a piece of wood. Note, It is a thing to be much lamented that even those who are separated to God are yet, when desolating judgments are abroad, often involved with others in the common calamity. <div eID="gen18331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18332" type="x-p"/> VI. Jerusalem came down slowly, and died a lingering death; for the famine contributed more to her destruction than any other judgment whatsoever. Upon this account the destruction of <hi type="italic">Jerusalem was greater than that of Sodom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.6">v. 6</reference>), for that was <hi type="italic">overthrown in a moment;</hi> one shower of fire and brimstone dispatched it; <hi type="italic">no hand staid on her;</hi> she did not endure any long siege, as Jerusalem has done; she fell immediately into the <hi type="italic">hands of the Lord,</hi> who strikes home at a blow, and did not <hi type="italic">fall into the hands of man,</hi> who, being weak, is long in doing execution, <reference osisRef="Judg.8.21">Judg. viii. 21</reference>. Jerusalem is kept many months upon the rack, in pain and misery, and dies by inches, dies so as to feel herself die. And, when the iniquity of Jerusalem is more aggravated than that of Sodom, no wonder that the punishment of it is so. Sodom never had the means of grace the Jerusalem had, the oracles of God and his prophets, and therefore the condemnation of Jerusalem will be <hi type="italic">more intolerable</hi> than that of Sodom, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.23-Matt.11.24">Matt. xi. 23, 24</reference>. The extremity of the famine is here set forth by two frightful instances of it:—1. The tedious deaths that it was the cause of (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.9">v. 9</reference>); many were slain with hunger, were famished to death, their stores being spent, and the public stores so nearly spent that they could not have any relief out of them. They were <hi type="italic">stricken through, for want of the fruits of the field;</hi> those who were starved were as sure to die as if they had been stabbed and stricken through; only their case was much more miserable. <hi type="italic">Those who are slain with the sword</hi> are soon put out of their pain; <hi type="italic">in a moment they go down to the grave,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.13">Job xxi. 13</reference>. They have not the terror of seeing death make its advances towards them, and scarcely feel it when the blow is given; it is but one sharp struggle, and the work is done. And, if we be ready for another world, we need not be afraid of a short passage to it; the quicker the better. But those who die by famine pine away; hunger preys upon their spirits and wastes them gradually; nay, and it frets their spirits, and fills them with vexation, and is as great a torture to the mind as to the body. There are <hi type="italic">bands in their death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.4">Ps. lxxiii. 4</reference>. 2. The barbarous murders that it was the occasion of (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">The hands of the pitiful women have</hi> first slain and then <hi type="italic">sodden their own children.</hi> This was lamented before (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">ch. ii. 20</reference>); and it was a thing to be greatly lamented that any should be so wicked as to do it and that they should be brought to such extremities as to be tempted to it. But this horrid effect of long sieges had been threatened in general (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Lev. xxvi. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">Deut. xxviii. 53</reference>), and particularly against Jerusalem in the siege of the Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="Jer.19.9">Jer. xix. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.10">Ezek. v. 10</reference>. The case was sad enough that they had not wherewithal to feed their children and make meat for them (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.4">v. 4</reference>), but much worse that they could find in their hearts to feed upon their children and make meat of them. I know not whether to make it an instance of the power of necessity or of the power of iniquity; but, as the Gentile idolaters were justly <hi type="italic">given up to vile affections</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.26">Rom. i. 26</reference>), so these Jewish idolaters, and the women particularly, who had <hi type="italic">made cakes to the queen of heaven</hi> and taught their children to do so too, were <hi type="italic">stripped of natural affection</hi> and that to their own children. Being thus left to <hi type="italic">dishonour their own nature</hi> was a righteous judgment upon them for the dishonour they had done to God. <div eID="gen18332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18333" type="x-p"/> VII. Jerusalem comes down utterly and wonderfully. 1. The destruction of Jerusalem is a complete destruction (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has accomplished his fury;</hi> he has made thorough work of it, has executed all that he purposed in wrath against Jerusalem, and has remitted no part of the sentence. He has poured out the full vials of his fierce anger, poured them out to the bottom, even the dregs of them. He has <hi type="italic">kindled a fire in Zion,</hi> which has not only consumed the houses, and levelled them with the ground, but, beyond what other fires do, has <hi type="italic">devoured the foundations thereof,</hi> as if they were to be no more built upon. 2. It is an amazing destruction, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.12">v. 12</reference>. It was a surprise to the kings of the earth, who are acquainted with, and inquisitive about, the state of their neighbours; nay, it was so to <hi type="italic">all the inhabitants of the world</hi> who knew Jerusalem, or had ever heard or read of it; they <hi type="italic">could not have believed that the adversary and enemy would ever enter into the gates of Jerusalem;</hi> for, (1.) They knew that Jerusalem was strongly fortified, not only by walls and bulwarks, but by the numbers and strength of its inhabitants; the strong hold of Zion was thought to be impregnable. (2.) They knew that it was the <hi type="italic">city of the great King,</hi> where the Lord of the whole earth had in a more peculiar manner his residence; it was the holy city, and therefore they thought that it was so much under the divine protection that it would be in vain for any of its enemies to make an attack upon it. (3.) They knew that many an attempt made upon it had been baffled, witness that of Sennacherib. They were therefore amazed when they heard of the Chaldeans making themselves masters of it, and concluded that it was certainly by an immediate hand of God that Jerusalem was given up to them; it was by a commission from him that the enemy broke through and entered the gates of Jerusalem.

<div eID="gen18333" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Cause of Jerusalem's Sorrows. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18334" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> For the sins of her prophets, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the iniquities of her priests, that have shed the blood of the just in the midst of her, <hi type="super">14</hi> They have wandered <hi type="italic">as</hi> blind <hi type="italic">men</hi> in the streets, they have polluted themselves with blood, so that men could not touch their garments. <hi type="super">15</hi> They cried unto them, Depart ye; <hi type="italic">it is</hi> unclean; depart, depart, touch not: when they fled away and wandered, they said among the heathen, They shall no more sojourn <hi type="italic">there.</hi> <hi type="super">16</hi> The anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath divided them; he will no more regard them: they respected not the persons of the priests, they favoured not the elders. <hi type="super">17</hi> As for us, our eyes as yet failed for our vain help: in our watching we have watched for a nation <hi type="italic">that</hi> could not save <hi type="italic">us.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> They hunt our steps, that we cannot go in our streets: our end is near, our days are fulfilled; for our end is come. <hi type="super">19</hi> Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of the heaven: they pursued us upon the mountains, they laid wait for us in the wilderness. <hi type="super">20</hi> The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , was taken in their pits, of whom we said, Under his shadow we shall live among the heathen. <div eID="gen18334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18335" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen18335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18336" type="x-p"/> I. The sins they were charged with, for which God brought this destruction upon them, and which served to justify God in it (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.13-Lam.4.14">v. 13, 14</reference>): It is <hi type="italic">for the sins of her prophets,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">iniquities of her priests.</hi> Not that the people were innocent; no, they <hi type="italic">loved to have it so</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jer. v. 31</reference>), and it was to please them that the prophets and priests did as they did; but the fault is chiefly laid upon them, who should have taught them better, should have reproved and admonished them, and told them what would be in the end hereof; of the hands of those watchmen who did not give them warning will their blood be required. Note, Nothing ripens a people more for ruin, nor fills the measure faster, than the sins of their priests and prophets. The particular sin charged upon them is persecution; the false prophets and corrupt priests joined their power and interest to <hi type="italic">shed the blood of the just in the midst of her,</hi> the blood of God's prophets and of those that adhered to them. They not only shed the blood of their innocent children, whom they sacrificed to Moloch, but the blood of the righteous men that were among them, whom they sacrificed to that more cruel idol of enmity to the truth and true religion. This was that sin which the Lord would not pardon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.4">2 Kings xxiv. 4</reference>) and which brought the last destruction upon Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.6">Jam. v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have condemned and killed the just.</hi> And the priests and prophets were the ringleaders in persecution, as in Christ's time the chief priests and scribes were the men that incensed the people against him, who otherwise would have persisted in their hosannas. Now these are those that <hi type="italic">wandered as blind men in the streets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.14">v. 14</reference>. They strayed from the paths of justice, were blind to every thing that is good, but to do evil they were quick-sighted. God says of corrupt judges, <hi type="italic">They know not, neither do they understand; they walk in darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Ps. lxxxii. 5</reference>); and Christ says of the corrupt teachers, <hi type="italic">They are blind leaders of the blind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.14">Matt. xv. 14</reference>. They have so <hi type="italic">polluted themselves with</hi> innocent <hi type="italic">blood,</hi> the blood of the saints, that <hi type="italic">men could not touch their garments;</hi> they made themselves odious to all about them, so that good men were as shy of touching them as of touching a dead body, which contracted a ceremonial pollution, or of touching the bloody clothes of one slain, which tender spirits care not to do. There is nothing that will make prophets and priests to be abhorred so much as a spirit of persecution. <div eID="gen18336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18337" type="x-p"/> II. The testimony of their neighbours produced in evidence against them, both to convict them of sin and to show the equity of God's proceedings against them. Some that have grown very impudent in sin boast that they <hi type="italic">care not what people say of them;</hi> but God, by the prophet, would have the Jews to take notice of what people said of them and what was the opinion of the standers by concerning them (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.15-Lam.4.16">v. 15, 16</reference>), what they said, nay, what <hi type="italic">they cried unto them,</hi> especially to the corrupt priests and prophets, <hi type="italic">among the heathen.</hi> 1. They upbraided them with their pretended purity, while they lived in all manner of real iniquity. They cried to them, "<hi type="italic">Depart you; it is unclean.</hi> You were so precise that you would not touch a Gentile, by cried, <hi type="italic">Depart, depart; stand by thyself; I am holier than thou,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Isa. lxv. 5</reference>. Thus the prosecutors of Christ would not go <hi type="italic">into the judgment-hall, lest they should be defiled.</hi> "But can you now keep the Gentiles from touching you, when God has delivered you into their hands? When you flee away and wander you will bid them stand off and not touch you, because they are unclean. But in vain; these serpents will not be charmed or enchanted thus; no, they will not <hi type="italic">respect the persons of the priests,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">favour the elders;</hi> the most venerable persons will to them be despicable." 2. They upbraided them with their sins, and the anger of God against them for their sins, and the direful effects of that anger. <hi type="italic">They cried to them, Depart you; it is unclean.</hi> They all cried out shame on them, and could easily foresee that God would not long suffer so provoking a people to continue in so good a land. They knew their <hi type="italic">statutes and judgments were righteous,</hi> and expected they should be <hi type="italic">a wise and understanding people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deut. iv. 6</reference>. But, when they saw them quite otherwise, they cried, <hi type="italic">Depart, depart;</hi> they soon read their doom, that the land would spue them out, as it had done their predecessors, and, when they saw the dispersed of <hi type="italic">Jacob fleeing and wandering,</hi> they told them of it. They said, Now <hi type="italic">the anger of the Lord has divided them,</hi> has dispersed them into all countries, because <hi type="italic">they respected not the persons of the priests,</hi> the pious priests that were among them, such as Zechariah the son of Jehoiada, Jeremiah, and others; neither did they <hi type="italic">favour the elders,</hi> but despised them and their authority when they went about to check them for their vicious courses. The very heathen foresaw that this would ruin them. 3. They triumphed in their ruin as irrecoverable. They said, when they saw them expelled out of their own land, "Now <hi type="italic">they shall no more sojourn there;</hi> they have bidden it a final farewell, never more to return to it, for <hi type="italic">God will no more regard them,</hi> and how then can they help themselves?" Herein they were mistaken. God had not cast them off, for all this. Yet thus much is intimated, that all about them observed them to be so very provoking to their God that there was not reason to expect any other than that they should be quite abandoned. <div eID="gen18337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18338" type="x-p"/> III. The despair which they themselves were almost brought to under their calamities. Having heard what they said concerning them <hi type="italic">among the heathen,</hi> let us now hear what they say concerning themselves (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">As for us,</hi> we look upon our case to be in a manner helpless. <hi type="italic">Our end is near</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.18">v. 18</reference>), the end both of our church and of our state; we are just at the brink of the ruin of both; nay, <hi type="italic">our end has come;</hi> we are utterly undone; a fatal final period is put to all our comforts; the days of our prosperity are fulfilled; they are numbered and finished." Thus their fears concurred with the hopes of their enemies that the <hi type="italic">Lord would no more regard them.</hi> For, 1. The refuges they fled to disappointed them. They looked for help from this and the other powerful ally, but to no purpose; it proved vain help. The succours they expected did not come in, or at least they had not the success they expected, and their eyes failed with looking for that which never came (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.17">v. 17</reference>); they <hi type="italic">watched in watching;</hi> they watched long, and with a great deal of earnestness and impatience, <hi type="italic">for a nation</hi> that promised them assistance, but failed them, and frustrated their expectation. They <hi type="italic">could not save them;</hi> they were too weak to contend with the Chaldean army and therefore retired. Help from creatures is vain help (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.11">Ps. lx. 11</reference>), and we may look for it till our eyes fail, till our hearts fail, and come short of it at last. 2. The persecutors they fled from overtook them and overcame them (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">They hunt our steps, that we cannot go in our streets.</hi> When the Chaldeans besieged the city they raised their batteries so high above the walls that they could command the town, and shoot at people as they went along the streets. They <hi type="italic">hunted them</hi> with their arrows from place to place. When the city was broken up, and all the men of war fled, their <hi type="italic">persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven</hi> when they fly upon their prey, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.19">v. 19</reference>. There was no escaping them; they <hi type="italic">pursued them upon the mountains,</hi> and, when they thought they had got clear of them, they fell into the hands of those that <hi type="italic">laid wait for them in the wilderness,</hi> to cut off their retreat, and to pick up stragglers. Nay, the king himself, though he may be supposed to have had all the advantages the exigence of the case would admit to favour his flight, yet could not escape, for divine vengeance pursued him with them, and then (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the Lord, was taken in their pits.</hi> Some apply it to Josiah, who was killed in battle by the king of Egypt; but it is rather to be understood of Zedekiah, who was the last king of the house of David, and who was pursued by the Chaldeans and seized in the plains of Jericho, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.5">Jer. xxxix. 5</reference>. He was <hi type="italic">the anointed of the Lord,</hi> heir of that family which God had appointed to the government. He was very much confided in by the Jewish state: <hi type="italic">They said, Under his shadow we shall live among the heathen.</hi> They promised themselves that the remnant which were left after Jeconiah's captivity should, under the protection of his government, yet again <hi type="italic">take root downward and bear fruit upward.</hi> They thought, though they were so reduced that they could not think of reigning over the heathen, as they had done, yet they might make a shift to live among them and not be insulted and pulled to pieces by them. Thus apt are sinking interests not only to catch at every twig, but to think it will recover them. Jerusalem died of a consumption, a flattering distemper. Even when she was ready to expire she formed some hopeful symptoms to herself, and on them grounded a hope that she should recover; but what came of it? The shadow under which they thought they should live proved like that of Jonah's gourd, which <hi type="italic">withered in a night.</hi> He that was <hi type="italic">the anointed of the Lord was taken in their pits,</hi> as if he had been but a beast of prey; so little account did they make of a person deemed sacred and not to be violated. Note, When we make any creature <hi type="italic">the breath of our nostrils,</hi> and promise ourselves that we shall live by it, it is just with God to stop that breath, and deprive us of the life we expected by it; for God will have the honour of being himself along <hi type="italic">our life and the length of our days.</hi>

<div eID="gen18338" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Comfort for Zion. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18339" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom, that dwellest in the land of Uz; the cup also shall pass through unto thee: thou shalt be drunken, and shalt make thyself naked. <hi type="super">22</hi> The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Zion; he will no more carry thee away into captivity: he will visit thine iniquity, O daughter of Edom; he will discover thy sins. <div eID="gen18339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18340" type="x-p"/> David's psalms of lamentation commonly conclude with some word of comfort, which is as life from the dead and light shining out of darkness; so does this lamentation here in this chapter. The people of God are now in great distress, their aspects all doleful, their prospects all frightful, and their ill-natured neighbours the Edomites insult over them and do all they can to exasperate their destroyers against them. Such was their violence against their brother Jacob (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.10">Obad. 10</reference>), such their spleen at Jerusalem, of which they cried, <hi type="italic">Rase it, rase it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Ps. cxxxvii. 7</reference>. Now it is here foretold, for the encouragement of God's people, <div eID="gen18340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18341" type="x-p"/> I. That an end shall be put to Zion's troubles (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">The punishment of they iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Zion!</hi> not the fulness of that punishment which it deserves, but of that which God has designed and determined to inflict, and which was necessary to answer the end, the glorifying of God's justice and the taking away of their sin. The captivity, which is <hi type="italic">the punishment of thy iniquity, is accomplished</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Isa. xl. 2</reference>), and <hi type="italic">he will no longer keep thee in captivity;</hi> so it may be read, as well as, <hi type="italic">he will no more carry thee into captivity;</hi> he will turn again thy captivity and work a glorious release for thee. Note, The troubles of God's people shall be continued no longer than till they have done their work for which they were sent. <div eID="gen18341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18342" type="x-p"/> II. That an end shall be put to Edom's triumphs. It is spoken ironically (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom!</hi> go on to insult over Zion in distress, till thou hast filled up the measure of thy iniquity. Do so; rejoice in thy own present exemption from the common fate of thy neighbours." This is like Solomon's upbraiding the young man with his ungoverned mirth (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Eccl. xi. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Rejoice, O young man! in thy youth;</hi> rejoice, if thou canst, when God comes to reckon with thee, and that he will do ere long. <hi type="italic">The cup</hi> of trembling, which it is now Jerusalem's turn to drink deeply of, <hi type="italic">shall pass through unto thee;</hi> it shall go round till it comes to be thy lot to pledge it." Note, This is a good reason why we should not insult over any who are in misery, because we ourselves also are in the body, and we know not how soon their case may be ours. But those who please themselves in the calamities of God's church must expect to have their doom, as aiders and abettors, with those that are instrumental in those calamities. The destruction of the Edomites was foretold by this prophet (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jer. xlix. 7</reference>. &c.), and the people of God must encourage themselves against their present rudeness and insolence with the prospect of it. 1. It will be a shameful destruction: "<hi type="italic">The cup</hi> that <hi type="italic">shall pass unto thee</hi> shall intoxicate thee" (and that is shame enough to any man); "<hi type="italic">thou shalt be drunken,</hi> quite infatuated, and at thy wits' end, shalt stagger in all thy counsels and stumble in all thy enterprises, and then, as Noah when he was drunk, <hi type="italic">thou shalt make thyself naked</hi> and expose thyself to contempt." Note, Those who ridicule God's people will justly be left to themselves to do that, some time or other, by which they will be made ridiculous. 2. It will be a righteous destruction. God will herein <hi type="italic">visit thy iniquity</hi> and <hi type="italic">discover thy sins;</hi> he will punish them, and, to justify himself therein, he will discover them, and make it to appear that he has just cause thus to proceed against them. Nay, the punishment of the sin shall so exactly answer the sin that it shall itself plainly discover it. Sometimes God does so visit the iniquity that he that runs may read the sin in the punishment. But, sooner or later, sin will be visited and discovered, and all the hidden works of darkness brought to light.  <chapter eID="Lam.4"/> <div eID="gen18342" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen18345" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18344" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">An Appeal to God; Complicated Sorrows. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18346" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Remember, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , what is come upon us: consider, and behold our reproach. <hi type="super">2</hi> Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens. <hi type="super">3</hi> We are orphans and fatherless, our mothers <hi type="italic">are</hi> as widows. <hi type="super">4</hi> We have drunken our water for money; our wood is sold unto us. <hi type="super">5</hi> Our necks <hi type="italic">are</hi> under persecution: we labour, <hi type="italic">and</hi> have no rest. <hi type="super">6</hi> We have given the hand <hi type="italic">to</hi> the Egyptians, <hi type="italic">and to</hi> the Assyrians, to be satisfied with bread. <hi type="super">7</hi> Our fathers have sinned, <hi type="italic">and are</hi> not; and we have borne their iniquities. <hi type="super">8</hi> Servants have ruled over us: <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that doth deliver <hi type="italic">us</hi> out of their hand. <hi type="super">9</hi> We gat our bread with <hi type="italic">the peril of</hi> our lives because of the sword of the wilderness. <hi type="super">10</hi> Our skin was black like an oven because of the terrible famine. <hi type="super">11</hi> They ravished the women in Zion, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the maids in the cities of Judah. <hi type="super">12</hi> Princes are hanged up by their hand: the faces of elders were not honoured. <hi type="super">13</hi> They took the young men to grind, and the children fell under the wood. <hi type="super">14</hi> The elders have ceased from the gate, the young men from their music. <hi type="super">15</hi> The joy of our heart is ceased; our dance is turned into mourning. <hi type="super">16</hi> The crown is fallen <hi type="italic">from</hi> our head: woe unto us, that we have sinned! <div eID="gen18346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18347" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted? let him pray;</hi> and let him in prayer pour out his complaint to God, and make known before him his trouble. The people of God do so here; being overwhelmed with grief, they give vent to their sorrows at the footstool of the throne of grace, and so give themselves ease. They complain not of evils feared, but of evils felt: "<hi type="italic">Remember what has come upon us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.5.1">v. 1</reference>. What was of old threatened against us, and was long in the coming, has now at length <hi type="italic">come upon us,</hi> and we are ready to sink under it. <hi type="italic">Remember what is</hi> past, <hi type="italic">consider and behold</hi> what is present, and <hi type="italic">let not all the trouble</hi> we are in <hi type="italic">seem little to thee,</hi> and not worth taking notice of," <reference osisRef="Neh.9.32">Neh. ix. 32</reference>. Note, As it is a great comfort to us, so it ought to be a sufficient one, in our troubles, that God sees, and considers, and remembers, all that <hi type="italic">has come upon us;</hi> and in our prayers we need only to recommend our case to his gracious and compassionate consideration. The one word in which all their grievances are summer up is <hi type="italic">reproach: Consider, and behold our reproach.</hi> The troubles they were in compared with their former dignity and plenty, were a greater reproach to them than they would have been to any other people, especially considering their relation to God and dependence upon him, and his former appearances for them; and therefore this they complain of very sensibly, because, as it was a reproach, it reflected upon the name and honour of that God who had owned them for his people. <hi type="italic">And what wilt thou do unto thy great name?</hi> <div eID="gen18347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18348" type="x-p"/> I. They acknowledge the reproach of sin which they bear, <hi type="italic">the reproach of their youth</hi> (which Ephraim bemoans himself for, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.19">Jer. xxxi. 19</reference>), of the early days of their nation. This comes in in the midst of their complaints (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.7">v. 7</reference>), but may well be put in the front of them: <hi type="italic">Our fathers have sinned and are not;</hi> they are dead and gone, but <hi type="italic">we have borne their iniquities.</hi> This is not here a peevish complaint, nor an imputation of unrighteousness to God, like that which we have, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.29">Jer. xxxi. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.2">Ezek. xviii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">The fathers did eat sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">the ways of the Lord are not equal.</hi> But it is a penitent confession of the sins of their ancestors, which they themselves also had persisted in, for which they now justly suffered; the judgments God brought upon them were so very great that it appeared that God had in them an eye to the sins of their ancestors (because they had not been remarkably punished in this world) as well as to their own sins; and thus God was justified both in his connivance at their ancestors (he <hi type="italic">laid up their iniquity for their children</hi>) and in his severity with them, on whom he visited that iniquity, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.35-Matt.23.36">Matt. xxiii. 35, 36</reference>. Thus they do here, 1. Submit themselves to the divine justice: "Lord, thou art just in all that is brought upon us, for we are a seed of evil doers, children of wrath, and heirs of the curse; we are sinful, and we have it by kind." Note, The sins which God looks back upon in punishing we must look back upon in repenting, and must take notice of all that which will help to justify God in correcting us. 2. They refer themselves to the divine pity: "Lord, <hi type="italic">our fathers have sinned,</hi> and we justly smart for their sins; but <hi type="italic">they are not;</hi> they were taken away from the evil to come; they lived not to see and share in these miseries that have <hi type="italic">come upon us,</hi> and we are left to <hi type="italic">bear their iniquities.</hi> Now, though herein God is righteous, yet it must be owned that our case is pitiable, and worthy of compassion." Note, If we be penitent and patient under what we suffer for the sins of our fathers, we may expect that he who punishes will pity, and will soon return in mercy to us. <div eID="gen18348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18349" type="x-p"/> II. They represent the reproach of trouble which they bear, in divers particulars, which tend much to their disgrace. <div eID="gen18349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18350" type="x-p"/> 1. They are disseised of that good land which God gave them, and their enemies have got possession of it, <reference osisRef="Lam.5.2">v. 2</reference>. Canaan was their inheritance; it was theirs by promise. God gave it to them and their seed, and they held it by grant from his crown, (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.21-Ps.136.22">Ps. cxxxvi. 21, 22</reference>); but now, "It is turned to strangers; those possess it who have no right to it, who are <hi type="italic">strangers to the commonwealth of Israel and aliens from the covenants of promise;</hi> they dwell in the houses that we built, and this is our reproach." It is the happiness of all God's spiritual Israel that the heavenly Canaan is an inheritance that they cannot be disseised of, that shall never be turned to strangers. <div eID="gen18350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18351" type="x-p"/> 2. Their state and nation are brought into a condition like that of widows and orphans (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We are fatherless</hi> (that is, helpless); we have none to protect us, to provide for us, to take any care of us. Our king, who is the father of the country, is cut off; nay, God our Father seems to have forsaken us and cast us off; <hi type="italic">our mothers,</hi> our cities, that were as fruitful mothers in Israel, <hi type="italic">are</hi> now <hi type="italic">as widows,</hi> are as wives whose husbands are dead, destitute of comfort, and exposed to wrong and injury, and this is our reproach; for we who made a figure are now looked on with contempt." <div eID="gen18351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18352" type="x-p"/> 3. They are put hard to it to provide necessaries for themselves and their families, whereas once they lived in abundance and had plenty of every thing. Water used to be free and easily come by, but now (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">We have drunk our water for money,</hi> and the saying is no longer true, <hi type="italic">Usus communis aquarum</hi>—<hi type="italic">Water is free to all.</hi> So hardly did their oppressors use them that they could not have a draught of fair water but they must purchase it either with money or with work. Formerly they had fuel too for the fetching; but now, "<hi type="italic">Our wood is sold to us,</hi> and we pay dearly for every faggot." Now were they punished for employing their children to gather wood for fire with which to <hi type="italic">bake cakes for the queen of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">Jer. vii. 18</reference>. They were perfectly proscribed by their oppressors, were forbidden the use both of fire and water, according to the ancient form, <hi type="italic">Interdico tibi aqua et igni</hi>—<hi type="italic">I forbid thee the use of water and fire.</hi> But what must they do for bread? Truly that was as hard to come at as any thing, for (1.) Some of them sold their liberty for it (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We have given the hand to the Egyptians and to the Assyrians,</hi> have made the best bargain we could with them, to serve them, that we might <hi type="italic">be satisfied with bread.</hi> We were glad to submit to the meanest employment, upon the hardest terms, to get a sorry livelihood; we have yielded ourselves to be their vassals, have parted with all to them, as the Egyptians did to Pharaoh in the years of famine, that we might have something for ourselves and families to subsist on." The neighbouring nations used to trade with Judah for wheat (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Ezek. xxvii. 17</reference>), for it was a fruitful land; but now it <hi type="italic">eats up the inhabitants,</hi> and they are glad to make court to the Egyptians and Assyrians. (2.) Others of them ventured their lives for it (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">We got our bread with the peril of our lives;</hi> when, being straitened by the siege and all provisions cut off, they either sallied or stole out of the city, to fetch in some supply, they were in danger of falling into the hands of the besiegers and being put to the sword, <hi type="italic">the sword of the wilderness</hi> it is called, or <hi type="italic">of the plain</hi> (for so the word signifies), the besiegers lying dispersed every where in the plains that were about the city. Let us take occasion hence to bless God for the plenty that we enjoy, that we get our bread so easily, scarcely with the sweat of our face, much less <hi type="italic">with the peril of our lives;</hi> and for the peace we enjoy, that we can go out, and enjoy not only the necessary productions, but the pleasures of the country, without any fear of <hi type="italic">the sword of the wilderness.</hi> <div eID="gen18352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18353" type="x-p"/> 4. Those are brought into slavery who were a free people, and not only their own masters, but masters of all about them, and this is as much as any thing their reproach (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Our necks are under</hi> the grievous and intolerable yoke of <hi type="italic">persecution</hi> (the iron yoke which Jeremiah foretold should be laid upon them, <reference osisRef="Jer.28.14">Jer. xxviii. 14</reference>); we are used like beasts in the yoke, that wholly serve their owners, and are at the command of their drivers. That which aggravated the servitude was, (1.) That their labours were incessant, like those of Israel in Egypt, who were daily tasked, nay, overtasked: <hi type="italic">We labour and have no rest,</hi> neither leave nor leisure to rest. The oxen in the yoke are unyoked at night and have rest; so they have, by a particular provision of the law, on the sabbath day; but the poor captives in Babylon, who were compelled to work for their living, <hi type="italic">laboured and had no rest,</hi> no night's rest, no sabbath-rest; they were quite tired out with continual toil. (2.) That their masters were insufferable (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Servants have ruled over us;</hi> and nothing is more vexatious than <hi type="italic">a servant when he reigns,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.30.22">Prov. xxx. 22</reference>. They were not only the great men of the Chaldeans that commanded them, but even the meanest of their servants abused them at pleasure, and insulted over them; and they must be at their beck too. The curse of Canaan had now become the doom of Judah: <hi type="italic">A servant of servants shall he be.</hi> They would not be ruled by their God, and by his servants the prophets, whose rule was gentle and gracious, and therefore justly are they ruled with rigour by their enemies and their servants. (3.) That they saw no probable way for the redress of their grievances: "<hi type="italic">There is none that doth deliver us out of their hand;</hi> not only none to rescue us out of our captivity, but none to check and restrain the insolence of the servants that abuse us and trample upon us," which one would think their masters should have done, because it was a usurpation of their authority; but, it should seem, they connived at it and encouraged it, and, as if they were not worthy of the correction of gentlemen, they are turned over to the footmen to be spurned by them. Well might they pray, <hi type="italic">Lord, consider and behold our reproach.</hi> <div eID="gen18353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18354" type="x-p"/> 5. Those who used to be feasted are now famished (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Our skin was black like an oven,</hi> dried and parched too, <hi type="italic">because of the terrible famine,</hi> the <hi type="italic">storms of famine</hi> (so the word is); for, though famine comes gradually upon a people, yet it comes violently, and bears down all before it, and there is no resisting it; and this also is their disgrace; hence we read of <hi type="italic">the reproach of famine,</hi> which in captivity their received among the heathen, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.30">Ezek. xxxvi. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen18354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18355" type="x-p"/> 6. All sorts of people, even those whose persons and characters were most inviolable, were abused and dishonoured. (1.) The <hi type="italic">women</hi> were <hi type="italic">ravished,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the women in Zion,</hi> that holy mountain, <reference osisRef="Lam.5.11">v. 11</reference>. The committing of such abominable wickednesses there is very justly and sadly complained of. (2.) The great men were not only put to death, but put to ignominious deaths. <hi type="italic">Princes were hanged,</hi> as if they had been slaves, <hi type="italic">by the hands</hi> of the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.12">v. 12</reference>), who took a pride in doing this barbarous execution with <hi type="italic">their own hands.</hi> Some think that the dead bodies of the princes, after they were slain with the sword, were hung up, as the bodies of Saul's sons, in disgrace to them, and as it were to expiate the nation's guilt. (3.) No respect was shown to magistrates and those in authority: <hi type="italic">The faces of elders,</hi> elders in age, elders in office, <hi type="italic">were not honoured.</hi> This will be particularly remembered against the Chaldeans another day. <reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">Isa. xlvii. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke.</hi> (4.) The tenderness of youth was no more considered than the gravity of old age (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">They took the young men to grind</hi> at the hand-mills, nay, perhaps at the horse-mills. <hi type="italic">The young men have carried the grist</hi> (so some), <hi type="italic">have carried the mill,</hi> or <hi type="italic">mill-stones,</hi> so others. They loaded them as if they had been beasts of burden, and so broke their backs while they were young, and made the rest of their lives the more miserable. Nay, they made <hi type="italic">the</hi> little <hi type="italic">children</hi> carry their wood home for fuel, and laid such burdens upon them that they <hi type="italic">fell</hi> down <hi type="italic">under</hi> them, so very inhuman were these cruel taskmasters! <div eID="gen18355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18356" type="x-p"/> 7. An end was put to all their gladness, and their joy was quite extinguished (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">The young men,</hi> who used to be disposed to mirth, have ceased <hi type="italic">from their music,</hi> have hung their harps upon the willow-trees. It does indeed well become old men to cease from their music; it is time to lay it by with a gracious contempt when <hi type="italic">all the daughters of music are brought low;</hi> but it speaks some great calamity upon a people when their young men are made to cease from it. It was so with the body of the people (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">The joy of their heart ceased;</hi> they never knew what joy was since the enemy came in upon them like a flood, for ever since <hi type="italic">deep called unto deep,</hi> and one wave flowed in upon the neck of another, so that they were quite overwhelmed: <hi type="italic">Our dance is turned into mourning,</hi> instead of leaping for joy, as formerly, we sink and lie down in sorrow. This may refer especially to the joy of their solemn feasts, and the dancing used in them (<reference osisRef="Judg.21.21">Judg. xxi. 21</reference>), which was not only modest, but sacred, dancing; this was <hi type="italic">turned into mourning,</hi> which was doubled on their festival days, in remembrance of their former pleasant things. <div eID="gen18356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18357" type="x-p"/> 8. An end was put to all their glory. (1.) The public administration of justice was their glory, but that was gone: <hi type="italic">The elders have ceased from the gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.14">v. 14</reference>); the course of justice, which used to run down like a river, is now stopped; the courts of justice, which used to be kept with so much solemnity, are put down; for the judges are slain, or carried captive. (2.) The royal dignity was their glory, but that also was gone: <hi type="italic">The crown has fallen from our head,</hi> not only the <hi type="italic">king</hi> himself fallen into disgrace, but <hi type="italic">the crown;</hi> he has no successor; the regalia are all lost. Note, Earthly crowns are fading falling things; but, blessed be God, there is <hi type="italic">a crown of glory that fades not away,</hi> that never falls, <hi type="italic">a kingdom that cannot be moved.</hi> Upon this complaint, but with reference to all the foregoing complaints, they make that penitent acknowledgment, "<hi type="italic">Woe unto us that we have sinned!</hi> Alas for us! Our case is very deplorable, and it is all owing to ourselves; we are undone, and, which aggravates the matter, we are undone by our own hands. God is righteous, for <hi type="italic">we have sinned.</hi>" Note, All our woes are owing to our own sin and folly. If <hi type="italic">the crown of our head be fallen</hi> (for so the words run), if we lose our excellency and become mean, we may thank ourselves, we have by our own iniquity profaned our crown and <hi type="italic">laid our honour in the dust.</hi>

<div eID="gen18357" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Unchangeableness of God; Prayer for Mercy and Grace. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18358" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> For this our heart is faint; for these <hi type="italic">things</hi> our eyes are dim. <hi type="super">18</hi> Because of the mountain of Zion, which is desolate, the foxes walk upon it. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thou, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , remainest for ever; thy throne from generation to generation. <hi type="super">20</hi> Wherefore dost thou forget us for ever, <hi type="italic">and</hi> forsake us so long time? <hi type="super">21</hi> Turn thou us unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old. <hi type="super">22</hi> But thou hast utterly rejected us; thou art very wroth against us. <div eID="gen18358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18359" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The people of God express the deep concern they had for the ruins of the temple, more than for any other of their calamities; the interests of God's house lay nearer their hearts than those of their own (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.17-Lam.5.18">v. 17, 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">For this our heart is faint,</hi> and sinks under the load of its own heaviness; <hi type="italic">for these things our eyes are dim,</hi> and our sight is gone, as is usual in a deliquium, or fainting fit. "It is <hi type="italic">because of the mountain of Zion, which is desolate,</hi> the holy mountain, and the temple built upon that mountain. For other desolations our hearts grieve and our eyes weep; but for this our hearts faint and our eyes are dim." Note, Nothing lies so heavily upon the spirits of good people as that which threatens the ruin of religion or weakens its interests; and it is a comfort if we can appeal to God that that afflicts us more than any temporal affliction to ourselves. "The people have polluted the <hi type="italic">mountain of Zion</hi> with their sins, and therefore God has justly made it <hi type="italic">desolate,</hi> to such a degree that <hi type="italic">the foxes walk upon it</hi> as freely and commonly as they do in the woods." It is sad indeed when the <hi type="italic">mountain of Zion</hi> has become <hi type="italic">a portion for foxes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.10">Ps. lxiii. 10</reference>); but sin had first made it so, <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.4">Ezek. xiii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen18359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18360" type="x-p"/> II. They comfort themselves with the doctrine of God's eternity, and the perpetuity of his government (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.19">v. 19</reference>): But <hi type="italic">thou, O Lord! remainest for ever.</hi> This they are taught to do by that psalm which is entitled, <hi type="italic">A prayer of the afflicted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.102.27-Ps.102.28">Ps. cii. 27, 28</reference>. When all our creature-comforts are removed from us, and our hearts fail us, we may then encourage ourselves with the belief, 1. Of God's eternity: <hi type="italic">Thou remainest for ever.</hi> What shakes the world gives no disturbance to him who made it; whatever revolutions there are on earth there is no change in the Eternal Mind; God is still the same, and <hi type="italic">remains for ever</hi> infinitely wise and holy, just and good; with him there is <hi type="italic">no variableness nor shadow of turning.</hi> 2. Of the never-failing continuance of his dominion: <hi type="italic">Thy throne is from generation to generation;</hi> the throne of glory, the throne of grace, and the throne of government, are all unchangeable, immovable; and this is matter of comfort to us when <hi type="italic">the crown has fallen from our head.</hi> When the thrones of princes, that should be our protectors, are brought to the dust, and buried in it, God's throne continues still; he still rules the world, and rules it for the good of the church. The Lord reigns, reigns for ever, even <hi type="italic">thy God, O Zion!</hi> <div eID="gen18360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18361" type="x-p"/> III. They humbly expostulate with God concerning the low condition they were now in, and the frowns of heaven they were now under (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Wherefore dost thou forsake us so long time,</hi> as if we were quite deprived of the tokens of thy presence? Wherefore dost thou defer our deliverance, as if thou hadst utterly abandoned us? Thou art the same, and, though the throne of thy sanctuary is demolished, thy throne in heaven is unshaken. But wilt thou not be the same to us?" Not as if they thought God had forgotten and forsaken them, much less feared his forgetting and forsaking them for ever; but thus they express the value they had for his favour and presence, which they thought it long that they were deprived of the evidence and comfort of. The <reference osisRef="Lam.5.22">last verse</reference> may be read as such an expostulation, and so the margin reads it: "<hi type="italic">For wilt thou utterly reject us? Wilt thou be perpetually wroth with us,</hi> not only not smile upon us and remember us in mercy, but frown upon us and lay us under the tokens of thy wrath, not only not draw nigh to us, but cast us out of thy presence and forbid us to draw nigh unto thee? How ill this be reconciled with thy goodness and faithfulness, and the stability of thy covenant?" We read it, "<hi type="italic">But thou hast rejected us;</hi> thou hast given us cause to fear that thou hast. Lord, how long shall we be in this temptation?" Note, Thou we may not quarrel with God, yet we may plead with him; and, though we may not conclude that he has cast off, yet we may (with the prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jer. xii. 1</reference>) humbly reason with him concerning his judgments, especially the continuance of the desolations of his sanctuary. <div eID="gen18361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18362" type="x-p"/> IV. They earnestly pray to God for mercy and grace: "Lord, do not reject <hi type="italic">us for ever,</hi> but <hi type="italic">turn thou us unto thee; renew our days,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Lam.5.21">v. 21</reference>. Though these words are not put last, yet the Rabbin, because they would not have the book to conclude with those melancholy words (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.22">v. 22</reference>), repeat this prayer again, that the sun may not set under a cloud, and so make these the last words both in writing and reading this chapter. They here pray, 1. For converting grace to prepare and qualify them for mercy: <hi type="italic">Turn us to thee, O Lord!</hi> They had complained that God had forsaken and forgotten them, and then their prayer is not, <hi type="italic">Turn thou to us,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">Turn us to thee,</hi> which implies an acknowledgment that the cause of the distance was in themselves. God never leaves any till they first leave him, nor stands afar off from any longer than while they stand afar off from him; if therefore he turn them to him in a way of duty, no doubt but he will quickly return to them in a way of mercy. This agrees with that repeated prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">Ps. lxxx. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.19">19</reference>), <hi type="italic">Turn us again, and then cause thy face to shine. Turn us</hi> from our idols to thyself, by a sincere repentance and reformation, <hi type="italic">and</hi> then <hi type="italic">we shall be turned.</hi> This implies a further acknowledgment of their own weakness and inability to turn themselves. There is in our nature a proneness to backslide from God, but no disposition to return to him till his grace works in us both <hi type="italic">to will and to do.</hi> So necessary is that grace that we may truly say, <hi type="italic">Turn us or we shall not be turned,</hi> but shall wander endlessly; and so powerful and effectual is that grace that we may as truly say, <hi type="italic">Turn us, and we shall be turned;</hi> for it is a day of power, almighty power, in which God's people are made a <hi type="italic">willing people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. 2. For restoring mercy: <hi type="italic">Turn us to thee,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">renew our days as of old,</hi> put us into the same happy state that our ancestors were in long ago and that they continued long in; let it be with us as it was <hi type="italic">at the first,</hi> and <hi type="italic">at the beginning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Isa. i. 26</reference>. Note, If God by his grace renew our hearts, he will be his favour <hi type="italic">renew our days,</hi> so that we shall <hi type="italic">renew our youth as the eagle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Ps. ciii. 5</reference>. Those that <hi type="italic">repent, and do their first works,</hi> shall rejoice, and recover their first comforts. God's mercies to his people have been <hi type="italic">ever of old</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.6">Ps. xxv. 6</reference>); and therefore they may hope, even then when he seems to have forsaken and forgotten them, that the mercy which was <hi type="italic">from everlasting</hi> will be <hi type="italic">to everlasting.</hi>  <chapter eID="Lam.5"/> <div eID="gen18362" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen18236" osisID="Lam" type="book"/>
